Chapter: On how love requires that the Beloved be singled out for love, and that no partner be associated with Him in it.

This is one of the requirements and rulings of sincere love, for the powers of love, once directed toward one object, leave no room in them for anything else. Among the sayings of people is: "There are not two loves in one heart, nor two lords in the heavens." And when the powers of love are divided among several objects, they inevitably weaken.

Consider His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah, and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ ﴿And rely upon Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

How He commanded him with taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of Allah), which implies singling Him out in obeying His command and prohibition out of love, awe and hope, for taqwa is not complete except by this. And [He commanded him with] following what was revealed to him, which implies abandoning everything other than that, and following the revealed text specifically. And [He commanded him] with tawakkul (trust in Allah), which involves the heart's reliance upon Him alone, its confidence in Him, and its tranquility in Him to the exclusion of others. Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body.﴾

So you find beneath this wording that the heart has only one direction: when it inclines toward one object, it does not incline toward another. A servant does not have two hearts, one by which he obeys Allah, follows His command and relies upon Him, and the other belonging to someone else. Rather, there is only one heart. If the servant does not single out his Lord with trust, love and taqwa, it will be diverted to something else.

Then he digressed from this to the point that He, glorified be He, did not make a man's wife his mother, and digressed from that to the point that He did not make his adopted son his son. So consider how excellent this foundation is, and this digression before which minds and intellects prostrate.

(Section: That naming is the right of the father, not of the mother)

This is something on which there is no dispute among people: if the two parents disagree about naming the child, the naming belongs to the father, and the hadiths mentioned earlier all indicate this. Just as the child is called after his father and not after his mother, so one says "so-and-so, son of so-and-so." Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾.

The child follows his mother in freedom and slavery, and follows his father in lineage (nasab). Naming is the identification of the lineage and of the one ascribed to it. In religion, the child follows the better of his two parents. Thus, identification is like teaching, and the 'aqiqah (sacrificial offering on the child's birth) is also the father's responsibility, not the mother's. The Prophet ﷺ said: "A child was born to me tonight, and I named him after my father Ibrahim." And a man naming his son is like a man naming his slave.

**(Benefit)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾ is evidence that whoever does not have the Messenger as closer to him than his own self is not among the believers. This closer standing (al-awliyyah) includes several matters:

Among them: that he loves him more than he loves himself, because closeness (al-awliyyah) is rooted in love, and a servant's own self is dearer to him than anyone else. Despite this, the Messenger must be closer to him than his self and dearer to him than it, and by this the name of faith is attained for him.

This closeness and love necessarily entail complete submission, obedience, contentment, acceptance, and the other requirements of love, such as being pleased with his judgment, accepting his command, and preferring him over everything else.

Among them: that the servant has no judgment over himself at all. Rather, the judgment over his self belongs to the Messenger ﷺ, and his judgment over it is greater than a master's judgment over his slave or a father's judgment over his child. So he has no disposal over himself whatsoever except what the Messenger, who is closer to him than himself, disposes of.

How strange it is that this closeness can be attained by a servant who has removed what the Messenger ﷺ brought from the position of arbitration, who is content with the judgment of another and at ease with it more than he is at ease with the Messenger ﷺ, and who claims that guidance is not to be sought from his niche (of revelation), but is received from the indications of reason, and that what he brought does not yield certainty, along with other sayings that include turning away from him and from what he brought, and referring knowledge that benefits to someone else. That is manifest error. There is no way to establish this closeness except by removing everything other than him, making him the authority in every matter, and presenting what anyone else has said to what he brought. If it is witnessed to be sound, it is accepted; if it is witnessed to be false, it is rejected. And if its testimony does not clearly show either soundness or falsehood, it is placed in the position of the narrations of the People of the Book, and it is withheld until it becomes clear which of the two is closer to it.

Whoever follows this method, his journey of migration (hijrah) is set right for him, his knowledge and his action are set right for him, and the faces of truth turn toward him from every direction.

**[Section: On his wives ﷺ]**

The first of them was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid al-Qurashiyyah al-Asadiyyah. He married her before prophethood, when she was forty years old. He did not marry another woman while she was alive. All his children, except Ibrahim, were from her. She supported him in prophethood, strove alongside him, and comforted him with her self and her wealth. Allah sent her greetings through Jibril, and this is a distinction not known for any woman other than her. She died three years before the Hijrah.

Then, a few days after her death, he married Sawdah bint Zam'ah al-Qurashiyyah, who gave her day (with the Prophet) to 'Aishah.

Then after her he married Umm 'Abdullah, 'Aishah al-Siddiqah, daughter of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), the one declared innocent from above the seven heavens, the beloved of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Aishah bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq. The angel showed her to him before the marriage, in a silk cloth, and said: "This is your wife." He married her in Shawwal when she was six years old, and he consummated the marriage with her in Shawwal in the first year of the Hijrah when she was nine years old. He did not marry a virgin other than her. Revelation did not come to him under the covering of any other woman. She was the dearest of creation to him. Her innocence was revealed from the heavens. The Ummah agreed on the disbelief of the one who accused her. She was the most learned and knowledgeable of his wives, indeed the most learned and knowledgeable of the women of the Ummah without qualification. The senior Companions of the Prophet ﷺ used to refer to her opinion and seek her rulings. It was said that she caused the Prophet ﷺ to have a miscarriage, but this is not established.

Then he married Hafsah bint 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu Dawud mentioned that he divorced her and then took her back.

Then he married Zaynab bint Khuzaymah ibn al-Harith al-Qaysiyyah from the Banu Hilal ibn 'Amir. She died in his house two months after he took her.

Then he married Umm Salamah, Hind bint Abi Umayyah al-Qurashiyyah al-Makhzumiyyah. The name of Abu Umayyah was Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah. She was the last of his wives to die.

It was also said that the last of them to die was Safiyyah.

There was disagreement about who arranged her marriage to him. Ibn Sa'd said in al-Tabaqat: Salamah ibn Abi Salamah arranged her marriage to him, to the exclusion of any other of her relatives. When the Prophet ﷺ married Salamah ibn Abi Salamah to Umamah bint Hamzah, over whom 'Ali, Ja'far, and Zayd had disputed, he said: "Have I repaid Salamah?" He said this because Salamah was the one who arranged his marriage, to the exclusion of her other relatives. This is mentioned in the biography of Salamah. Then it is mentioned in the biography of Umm Salamah, from al-Waqidi: Mujama' ibn Ya'qub narrated to me, from Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, from his father, that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proposed to Umm Salamah through her son 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married her, while he was then a small boy."

Imam Ahmad said in the Musnad: 'Affan narrated to us, Hammad ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, Thabit narrated to us, who said: Ibn 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah narrated to me, from his father, "from Umm Salamah, that when her waiting period (iddah) from Abu Salamah ended, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to her. She said: 'Welcome to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I am a woman who is jealous, and I have children, and none of my guardians is present...' — the hadith — and in it she said to her son 'Umar: 'Stand up and marry the Messenger of Allah ﷺ,' and he married him." But there is a problem with this. This 'Umar was nine years old when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, as Ibn Sa'd mentioned. The Prophet ﷺ married her in Shawwal of the fourth year, so he would have been three years old at that time, and a child of that age does not conduct a marriage contract. Ibn Sa'd and others said this. When this was said to Imam Ahmad, he said: "Who says that 'Umar was a small child?"

Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: Perhaps Ahmad said this before he learned the exact measure of his age, and a group of historians, including Ibn Sa'd and others, have mentioned his exact age.

It has also been said that the one who gave her in marriage to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was her paternal cousin 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and the hadith (reads): "Stand up, O 'Umar, and marry the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The lineage of 'Umar and the lineage of Umm Salamah meet at Ka'b. 'Umar is ibn al-Khattab ibn Nufayl ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn Riyah ibn 'Abdullah ibn Qurt ibn Razah ibn 'Adi ibn Ka'b, and Umm Salamah is bint Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar ibn Makhzum ibn Yaqzah ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b. So the name of her son 'Umar coincided with his name, and she said: "Stand up, O 'Umar, and marry the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Some narrators thought that he was her son, so they narrated it by meaning and said: "She said to her son," and they forgot that this was impossible for him because of his young age. A similar error was made by some jurists regarding this hadith, and in their narration the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Stand up, O boy, and marry your mother." Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: We do not know this wording in this hadith. He said: Even if it is established, it may be that he said it jokingly to the small child, since he was then three years old. For the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married her in the fourth year, and he died when 'Umar was nine years old. And the marriage of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not depend on a guardian (wali).

Ibn 'Aqil said: The apparent meaning of Ahmad's statement is that the Prophet ﷺ's marriage does not require a guardian, and that this is one of his special privileges.

Then he married Zaynab bint Jahsh from the Banu Asad ibn Khuzaymah, who was the daughter of his paternal aunt Umaymah. Concerning her the words of Allah, Exalted are You, were revealed: ﴿So when Zayd had no more need of her, We married her to you.﴾

Because of this she used to boast over the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and say: "Your families married you off, but Allah married me off from above the seven heavens."

Among her special distinctions is that Allah, glorified and exalted, was himself her guardian who gave her in marriage to His Messenger from above His heavens. She died at the beginning of the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. She was first married to Zayd ibn Harithah, whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had adopted. When Zayd divorced her, Allah, Exalted, married her to him so that his Ummah would follow him in marrying the wives of those whom they adopt.

He ﷺ also married Juwayriyah bint al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar al-Mustaliqiyyah, who was among the captives of the Banu al-Mustaliq. She came to him seeking his help with her kitabah (a contract by which a slave purchases freedom in installments), so he paid her kitabah on her behalf and married her.

Then he married Umm Habibah, whose name was Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan Sakhr ibn Harb al-Qurashiyyah al-Umawiyyah. It was also said that her name was Hind. He married her while she was in the land of Abyssinia as a muhajirah (emigrant), and al-Najashi gave her dowry on his behalf, four hundred dinars. She was brought to him from there, and she died in the days of her brother Mu'awiyah.

This is the well-known and widely transmitted account among the people of biographies (siyar) and histories, and for them it is on the same level as his marriage to Khadijah in Makkah, to Hafsah in Madinah, and to Safiyyah after Khaybar.

As for the hadith of 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Zumayl, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Abu Sufyan said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'I ask you three things,' and he gave him them, among them: 'And with me is the most beautiful of the Arabs, Umm Habibah; I will marry her to you.'"

This hadith is an obvious error. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: It is undoubtedly fabricated (mawdu'), and 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar lied in it. Ibn al-Jawzi said about this hadith: It is an error by some of the narrators, without any doubt or hesitation, and they have accused 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar of it, because the historians are unanimous that Umm Habibah was married to 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh, bore him children, and emigrated with him to the land of Abyssinia while both of them were Muslims. Then he (Ibn Jahsh) became a Christian, while Umm Habibah remained steadfast in her Islam. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to al-Najashi to propose to her on his behalf, and he married her to him and gave a dowry on his behalf. That was in the seventh year of the Hijrah. Abu Sufyan came during the time of the truce and entered upon her, and she folded up the bedding of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that he would not sit on it. There is no disagreement that Abu Sufyan and Mu'awiyah became Muslims at the conquest of Makkah in the eighth year.

Also, in this hadith he said to him: "Will you appoint me (as commander) so that I may fight the disbelievers as I used to fight the Muslims?" He said: "Yes." But it is not known that the Prophet ﷺ ever appointed Abu Sufyan as a commander at all.

He ﷺ also married Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab, chief of the Banu al-Nadir, from the descendants of Harun ibn 'Imran, the brother of Musa. So she was the daughter of a prophet and the wife of a prophet, and she was among the most beautiful women of the worlds. She had become a slave-girl (amah) to him from the spoils (al-safi), and he freed her and made her freedom her dowry. Thus this became a sunnah for the Ummah until the Day of Resurrection: that a man frees his slave-girl and makes her freedom her dowry, so that she becomes his wife by that. If he says: "I have freed my slave-girl and made her freedom her dowry," or says: "I have made the freedom of my slave-girl her dowry," then the emancipation and the marriage are valid, and she becomes his wife without needing to renew the contract or a guardian. This is the apparent position of Ahmad and many of the people of hadith.

But a group said: This is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, one of the things Allah granted him in marriage, to the exclusion of the Ummah. This is the view of the three imams and those who agree with them. The correct view is the first, because the default is non-exclusivity until evidence establishes exclusivity. Allah, glorified is He, when He made it specific to him to marry a woman who gave herself to him, said about her: ﴿a privilege for you alone, excluding the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50].

He did not say this about the freed slave-girl, nor did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say it in order to cut off the Ummah's following of him in that. Allah, glorified is He, permitted him to marry the wife of the one he had adopted, so that there would be no hardship upon the Ummah in marrying the wives of those whom they adopt. This indicates that when he marries in a certain way, his Ummah may follow him in it, unless a text from Allah and His Messenger specifies exclusivity and cuts off the following. This is clear.

The full argumentation for this question and its detailed proof, and that the permissibility of such a thing is what the principles and analogy require, has another place, and we have only drawn attention to it briefly.

Then he married Maymunah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah, and she was the last woman he married. He married her in Makkah during the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the make-up 'umrah), after he had come out of ihram from it according to the correct view.

It was also said that he married her before he came out of ihram. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, but he was mistaken, may Allah be pleased with him. For the envoy between them in the marriage, who knew the story best of all creation, was Abu Rafi', and he reported that he married her while he was out of ihram, and said: "I was the envoy between them. Ibn 'Abbas at that time was about ten years old or a little more, and he was absent from the event and did not attend it. Abu Rafi' was an adult man, and the story unfolded through him, and he knew it best."

It is not hidden that such a preference necessitates giving precedence (to Abu Rafi's account). She died in the days of Mu'awiyah, and her grave is at Sarif.

It has been said: Among his wives was Rayhanah bint Zayd al-Nadriyyah. It was also said: she was al-Qurazhiyyah. She was captured on the day of the Banu Qurayzah, and she became the Prophet of Allah's ﷺ share (safiyy), so he freed her and married her. Then he divorced her with one divorce, and then took her back.

But a group said: Rather, she was his slave-girl, and he used to have intercourse with her by right of ownership until he died and left her. So she is counted among the concubines (saraary), not among the wives. The first view is the choice of al-Waqidi, and Sharaf al-Din al-Dimyati agreed with him and said: It is the most established view among the people of knowledge. In what he said there is room for examination, for what is known is that she was among his concubines and slave-girls. And Allah knows best.

These are his wives who are well known, those he consummated marriage with. As for the women who proposed to him but whom he did not marry, and the woman who gave herself to him but whom he did not marry, they number about four or five. Some have said they were thirty women. But those who know his biography and circumstances (ﷺ) do not recognize this and actually deny it. What is known among them is that he sent for the woman of the Jawn (al-Jawniyya) in order to marry her. He entered upon her to propose, and she sought refuge from him, so he granted her refuge and did not marry her. The same is true of al-Kalbiyya, and of the woman in whose side (kashh) he saw whiteness, so he did not consummate marriage with her. And the woman who gave herself to him, whom he then married to another man in exchange for portions of the Qur'an. This is the transmitted report, and God knows best.

There is no disagreement that he (ﷺ) died leaving nine wives, and he used to divide his time among eight of them: 'A'isha, Hafsa, Zaynab bint Jahsh, Umm Salama, Safiyya, Umm Habiba, Maymuna, Sawda, and Juwayriyya.

The first of his wives to join him after his death (ﷺ) was Zaynab bint Jahsh, in the year twenty (AH). The last of them to die was Umm Salama, in the year sixty-two (AH), during the caliphate of Yazid. And God knows best.

[Section: On the brotherhood (mu'akhah, the bond of fraternity) between the Emigrants and the Helpers]

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) established brotherhood between the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and the Helpers (Ansar) in the house of Anas ibn Malik. They were ninety men, half of them from the Emigrants and half from the Helpers. He bound them together in brotherhood on the basis of mutual support, and they would inherit from one another after death, to the exclusion of blood relatives, until the battle of Badr. When God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another in the Book of God﴾, He returned inheritance to kinship, to the exclusion of the bond of brotherhood.

It has also been said that he established a second brotherhood among the Emigrants themselves, one with another, and in it he took Ali as a brother for himself. The first established brotherhood is the more firmly confirmed. The Emigrants were sufficient in the brotherhood of Islam, the brotherhood of their dwelling, and the kinship of lineage, and did not need a formal bond of brotherhood, unlike the Emigrants with the Helpers. Had he established brotherhood among the Emigrants, the most entitled of people to his brotherhood would have been the dearest of creation to him, his companion in the migration, his intimate companion in the cave, and the best of the Companions and the most honored by him: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. He had said: "If I were to take a close friend (khalil) from among the people of the earth, I would have taken Abu Bakr as a close friend, but the brotherhood of Islam is superior."

In another wording: "But my brother and my companion." This brotherhood in Islam, though it is general, is as he said: "I wish that we had seen our brothers." They said: "Are we not your brothers?" He said: "You are my Companions, and my brothers are a people who will come after me, who will believe in me though they have not seen me."

So for al-Siddiq there is, from this brotherhood, its highest rank, just as he has from companionship its highest rank. The Companions have both the brotherhood and the distinction of companionship, while their followers after them have the brotherhood without the distinction of companionship.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 33, verses 7–8:

So when the truthful (al-sadiqun) are questioned and called to account for their truthfulness, what then of the liars?

Muqatil said: "The Exalted says: We took their covenant so that Allah may question the truthful, meaning the prophets, about the conveying of the message." And Mujahid said: "He questions those who convey and deliver from the messengers, meaning: did they convey on their behalf, just as the messengers are questioned: did they convey from Allah, the Exalted?"

The verified position (al-tahqiq): the verse encompasses both of these meanings. The truthful are the messengers and those who convey on their behalf. So the messengers are questioned about the conveying of His messages, and those who convey on their behalf are questioned about conveying what the messengers conveyed to them. Then those to whom the message reached are questioned about what they answered the messengers with, as the Exalted said:

﴿And on the day He calls them and says, "What did you answer the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 33, verses 7–8:

So when the truthful (al-sadiqun) are questioned and called to account for their truthfulness, what then of the liars?

Muqatil said: "The Exalted says: We took their covenant so that Allah may question the truthful, meaning the prophets, about the conveying of the message." And Mujahid said: "He questions those who convey and deliver from the messengers, meaning: did they convey on their behalf, just as the messengers are questioned: did they convey from Allah, the Exalted?"

The verified position (al-tahqiq): the verse encompasses both of these meanings. The truthful are the messengers and those who convey on their behalf. So the messengers are questioned about the conveying of His messages, and those who convey on their behalf are questioned about conveying what the messengers conveyed to them. Then those to whom the message reached are questioned about what they answered the messengers with, as the Exalted said:

﴿And on the day He calls them and says, "What did you answer the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 33, verses 16–17:

The one who flees thinks that by fleeing he will prolong his life, so that he enjoys living. But God, glory be to Him, has refuted this assumption, saying:

﴿Say: "Fleeing will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing; and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16].

So God informed that fleeing from death in martyrdom does not benefit; there is no profit in it. And even if it were to benefit, it would benefit only a little, since death is unavoidable for him. Through this little he would lose what is better and more beneficial for him: the life of the martyr with his Lord.

Then He said: ﴿Who is it that can protect you from God if He intends for you harm, or intends for you mercy? And they will not find for themselves, other than God, any protector or any helper.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 17].

So He, glory be to Him, informed that no one can protect the servant from God if He intends for him harm other than the death from which he fled. For he fled from death because it was distressing to him, and God, glory be to Him, informed that if He intends for him a harm other than it, no one can protect him from God. He may flee from what distresses him, such as being killed in the way of God, and then fall into what distresses him that is greater than it.

If this is the case regarding the calamity of the self, then the matter is likewise regarding the calamity of wealth, honor and body. For whoever withholds his wealth from spending it in the way of God, the Exalted, and in raising His word, God will deprive him of it, or will cause him to spend it on what benefits him neither in this world nor in the next, rather on what returns to him with harm, both swiftly and later. And if he holds it back and hoards it, He prevents him from enjoying it and transfers it to another.

Thus its pleasure belongs to another, and its burden is upon him who left it behind. Likewise, whoever pampers his body and his honor and prefers his ease over toil for God and in His way, God, glory be to Him, will cause him toil many times over in other than His way and His good pleasure. This is a matter that people know from experience.

(Benefit)

Some of the wise said in his advice:

"Keep to the people of generosity and courage, for they are the people of good opinion of God. Courage is a shield for a man against hardships, and cowardice is an aid that a man gives his enemy against himself. It is an army and a weapon that he gives his enemy so that he may fight him with it."

The Arabs have said: "Courage is protection, and cowardice is a slaying." And God, glory be to Him, has refuted the hopes of cowards in their assumption that their cowardice will save them from killing and death. God, Exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Fleeing will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16]

The poet said well [he is Qutari ibn al-Fujaa'a al-Sari]:

(I say to her when the heroes have scattered in fragments, "Woe to you, you will not be frightened.")

(For if you were to ask for the survival of a single day beyond the term appointed for you, you would not be obeyed.)

(So patience in the field of death, patience, for attaining immortality is not within reach.)

(And the garment of life is not a garment of honor, so as to shelter from the brother of abasement the reed-pen.)

(The path of death is the goal of every living thing, and its summoner calls to the people of the earth.)

(Whoever is not taken before his time will grow weary and grow old, and fate will bring him to an end.)

(And there is no good for a man in a life when he is counted among the discarded goods.)

Consider this in the battles of war, that whoever is killed while retreating is more numerous than whoever is killed while advancing. And in the counsel of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to Ibn al-Walid:

"Be eager for death, and life will be granted to you."

Khalid ibn al-Walid said:

"I have attended such-and-such engagements in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam, and there is not a place on my body but it has a spear-thrust or a sword-strike in it, and here I am, dying on my bed. May the eyes of cowards never sleep."

There is no doubt for any intelligent person that meeting death when it comes to you is better than turning your back to it. And God knows best. Hassan ibn Thabit clarified this, saying:

(We are not those whose wounds bleed on the backs, but rather on our feet the blood drips.)

Another, verifying this meaning, said:

(Forbidden are the necks of my horses upon the spears, and bloodied are their breasts and throats.)

(It is forbidden for our spears to thrust into a retreating man, and from them the chests break against the chests.)

They used to take pride in dying other than on a bed. When the news of the killing of his brother Mus'ab reached Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, he said:

"If he is killed, his brother and his father and his paternal uncle were killed. By God, we do not die a natural death, but our death is by the spears and under the shade of swords." [Then he quoted the words of the poet:]

(And our souls find the deaths sweet, while another time it leaves what it has not tasted.)

[And in such a vein al-Samaw'al of Kadiya says, in al-Hamasa:]

(No leader of ours died on his bed, nor was any of us slain without avenging.)

(Our souls flow along the edges of the swords, and they flow only by the swords.)

(And we are a people who do not regard killing as a disgrace, when Amir and Salul see it.)

(When our swords fall short, their joining is our steps toward our enemies, so they extend.)

Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Tahir ibn al-Husayn al-Khuza'i said:

(You are not for fragrance, nor for wine, nor for the neighbor's comfort.)

(So if you now want a place for me, it is between swords and spears.)

(You see a young man beneath the shade of the spears, exchanging souls for souls.)

Even if courage had no other merit than that the brave man's reputation and name ward off from him people's harm and prevent them from advancing against him, it would suffice as honor and excellence, as 'Amr ibn Baraqa said, and he was a renowned daredevil known for boldness and steadfastness:

(You have lied, by the House of God, you will not take them by force, as long as the sword remains.)

(When you gather a discerning heart and a sharp blade, and a fierce spirited nose, injustices will avoid you.)

(You have lied, by the House of God, you will not take them by force, as long as the sword remains.)

(When you gather a discerning heart and a sharp blade, and a fierce spirited nose, injustices will avoid you.)

**(Benefit)**

When Messengers are sent to people, they are faced with one of two situations. Either one of them says, "I have believed," or he does not believe and remains in his misdeeds and disbelief. Both cases must be tested.

As for the one who says, "I have believed," his Lord will certainly test him and try him, so that it becomes clear whether he is truthful in his words, "I have believed," or a liar. If he is a liar, he turns back on his heels and flees the trial, just as he flees from the punishment of Allah. If he is truthful, he holds firm to his words, and the trial and testing only increase him in faith upon his faith. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly." And it increased them only in faith and submission.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22].

As for the one who does not believe, he will be tested in the Hereafter with punishment, and he will be afflicted by it, and this is the greater of the two trials. This is so if he is spared being tested by the punishment of this world and its calamities, and by its penalties which Allah inflicted upon those who did not follow His Messengers and disobeyed them. Therefore a trial is certain in this abode, in the barzakh (the intermediate realm), and on the Day of Resurrection for every person. But the believer's trial is lighter and his affliction easier, for Allah repels [harm] from him through faith, bears [some of his burden] for him because of it, and grants him patience, steadfastness, contentment and submission, by which his trial becomes easy for him.

As for the disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked, their trial and affliction are severe and lasting. So the trial of the believer is light and ends, while the trial of the disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked is severe and continuous.

Pain and trial are certain for every soul, whether it believes or disbelieves. But the believer experiences pain in this world at the outset, and then the outcome of both this world and the Hereafter is his. The disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked experience pleasure and bliss at the outset, and then they come to pain. So no one should hope to be entirely free of hardship and pain.

**(Section: On the mention of the fragrance of Paradise and the distance from which it is perceived)**

Al-Tabarani said: Musa ibn Hazim al-Asbahani narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Bukayr al-Hadrami narrated to us, Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah al-Fazari narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Amr, from Mujahid, from Junadah ibn Abi Umayyah, from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"Whoever kills a person from among the dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection) will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is perceived from a distance of one hundred years."

Al-Bukhari also narrated it in his Sahih, from Qays ibn Hafs, from Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Amr al-Fuqaymi, from Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr, without mentioning Junadah between them, and he said: "...is perceived from a distance of forty years."

Al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Sulayman, that is al-Basri, narrated to us, from Ibn Ajlan, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"Beware! Whoever kills a person under covenant (mu'ahad) who has the protection of Allah and His Messenger, has indeed broken the protection of Allah, and he will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is perceived from a distance of seventy autumns."

He said: "On this topic there is also a report from Abu Bakrah. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is hasan sahih (good and sound)." Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahid said: "Its isnad, in my view, meets the conditions of the sahih." I say: Al-Tabarani also narrated it from the hadith of Isa ibn Yunus, from Awf al-A'rabi, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever kills a person under covenant unjustly, will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, and the fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of one hundred years."

Al-Tabarani also said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, from Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan or another, from Abu Bakrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah say:

"The fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of one hundred years."

These wordings do not contradict one another in any way.

Both [al-Bukhari and Muslim] have also related in the two Sahihs (Sahihayn, the two authentic collections) from the hadith of Anas, who said: My uncle did not witness Badr with the Messenger of Allah. He said: "It grieved him." He said: "The first battle with the Messenger of Allah that I missed..." He said: "If Allah shows me another occasion to be with the Messenger of Allah, Allah will see what I do." He said: "So he feared to say anything other than that." He said: "Then he witnessed Uhud with the Messenger of Allah." He said: "Then he met Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and said to him, 'Where?' He said: 'Aha! By the fragrance of Paradise! I perceive it beyond Uhud.'" He said: "So he fought them until he was killed." He said: "He was found to have over eighty wounds on his body, from strikes, stabs and arrows." His sister, Amat al-Rubay' bint al-Nadr, said: "I did not recognise my brother except by his fingertips." And this verse was revealed: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted Allah upon.﴾ He said: "They used to think it was revealed concerning him and his companions."

The fragrance of Paradise is of two kinds. One is a fragrance found in this world, which souls sometimes smell, though people do not perceive it. The other is a fragrance perceived by the sense of smell of bodies, just as one smells the scents of flowers and other things. The people of Paradise share in perceiving this in the Hereafter, both near and far. In this world, it may be perceived by whomever Allah wills from among His prophets and messengers. What Anas ibn al-Nadr found may belong to either category, and Allah knows best.

Abu Nu'aym said: Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Mu'adhdhin narrated to us, Abd al-Wahid ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, al-Rabi' ibn Badr informed us, Harun ibn Riyab narrated to us, from Mujahid, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "The fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of five hundred years."

Al-Tabarani said: Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Hadrami narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Tarif narrated to us, my father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, Jabir al-Ju'fi related to me, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of a thousand years, and by Allah, an undutiful son and one who severs the ties of kinship will not smell it."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi said in his Musnad: Shu'bah narrated to us, from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever claims to be the son of someone other than his father will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is perceived from a distance of five hundred years. Allah, glorified is He, has indeed shown His servants in this abode some traces of Paradise and a sample of it: its pleasant fragrance, its desirable delights, its beautiful sights, its good fruits, its bliss, its joy, and the coolness of the eye."

**[Section: On the Battle of the Trench (Ghazwat al-Khandaq)]**

It took place in the fifth year after the Hijrah, in Shawwal, according to the more correct of the two opinions, since there is no dispute that the Battle of Uhud was in Shawwal of the third year. The polytheists had promised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a meeting in the following year, which was the fourth year, but then they broke their promise because of the drought of that year, and they returned. When the fifth year came, they came to fight him. This is the view of the people of the biographies and the military campaigns (Ahl al-Siyar wa al-Maghazi).

Musa ibn Uqbah differed with them and said: "Rather, it was in the fourth year." Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: "This is the correct view about which there is no doubt." He argued for it with the hadith of Ibn Umar in the Sahihayn, that he was presented to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud when he was fourteen years old, and he was not permitted [to fight]; then he was presented to him on the day of the Trench when he was fifteen years old, and he was permitted.

He said: "So it is established that there was only one year between them."

This was answered with two replies. The first: Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him back because he considered him too young for fighting, and permitted him when he reached the age at which he was seen to be capable. There is nothing in this that denies that the interval between them could have been a year or so.

The second: Perhaps the Battle of Uhud was at the beginning of his fourteenth year, and the Battle of the Trench at the end of his fifteenth year.

**[The cause of the Battle of the Trench]**

The cause of the Battle of the Trench was that when the Jews saw the victory of the polytheists over the Muslims at Uhud, and when they learned of Abu Sufyan's appointment to attack the Muslims, he went out for that purpose. Then he returned in the following year. The leaders of the Jews, such as Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Kinanah ibn al-Rabi' and others, went out to the Quraysh in Makkah to incite them to attack the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to stir them up against him, and they promised them on their own behalf to support them. The Quraysh responded to them. Then they went out to Ghatafan and called them, and they responded to them. Then they went around among the Arab tribes calling them to this, and whoever responded, responded. So the Quraysh went out, led by Abu Sufyan, with four thousand men. The Banu Sulaym joined them at Marr al-Zahran. The Banu Asad, Fazarah, Ashja' and Banu Murrah went out, and Ghatafan came with their leader Uyaynah ibn Hisn. The number of disbelievers who reached the Trench was ten thousand.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of their march against him, he consulted the Companions. Salman al-Farisi advised him to dig a trench which would stand between the enemy and Madinah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered it, and the Muslims hastened to it, and he himself worked in it. They also hastened to pre-empt the assault of the disbelievers against them. In the digging of the trench there were signs of his prophethood and marks of his messengership, of which the reports are widely transmitted. The digging of the Trench was in front of Sal', and Sal' is a mountain behind the backs of the Muslims, while the Trench lay between them and the disbelievers.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with three thousand Muslims. He was protected by the mountain at his back, and by the Trench in front of them.

Ibn Ishaq said: "He went out with seven hundred," but this is an error, derived from [the number who went out] at Uhud.

The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the women and children to be placed in the fortified towers of Madinah, and he appointed Ibn Umm Maktum as their deputy.

Huyayy ibn Akhtab set out to the Banu Qurayzah and approached their fortress. Ka'b ibn Asad refused to open it for him, but he kept speaking to him until he opened it for him. When he entered upon him, he said: "I have come to you with the honour of the age. I have come to you with the Quraysh, Ghatafan and Asad, under their commanders, to fight Muhammad." Ka'b said: "By Allah, you have come to me with the humiliation of the age, and with a cloud whose water has been poured out; it thunders and flashes, but there is nothing in it."

He kept at him until he broke the covenant between himself and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and joined the polytheists in fighting him. The polytheists rejoiced at this. Ka'b stipulated with Huyayy that if they did not overcome Muhammad, he would come and enter his fortress with him, and suffer what he suffered. Huyayy agreed to this and fulfilled it to him.

News of the Banu Qurayzah and their breaking of the covenant reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he sent to them al-Sa'dayn (Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn Ubadah), Khawwat ibn Jubayr, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah, to find out whether they were still upholding their covenant or had broken it. When they drew near to them, they found them in the worst condition: they openly reviled them with abuse and hostility, and they insulted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So they withdrew from them and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) using indirect words to inform him that they had broken the covenant and acted treacherously. This was grievous to the Muslims. At that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Allahu Akbar! Rejoice, O assembly of Muslims!"

The trial intensified, hypocrisy appeared, and some of the Banu Harithah asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to go back to Madinah, saying: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed, though they were not exposed. They only intended to flee.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13].

The Banu Salamah were inclined to cowardice, but then Allah made both groups firm.

The polytheists remained besieging the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a month, and there was no fighting between them, because of what Allah had placed of the Trench between them and the Muslims, except that some horsemen of the Quraysh, among them Amr ibn Abd Wudd and a group with him, came towards the Trench. When they stood at it, they said: "This is a stratagem which the Arabs did not know." Then they aimed for a narrow place in the Trench, forced their way across it, and their horses roamed in the salt flat between the Trench and Sal'. They called for single combat, and Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) volunteered for Amr. He fought him, and Allah killed him at his hands. He had been one of the bravest and champions of the polytheists. The rest fled back to their companions. (The war-cry of the Muslims that day was: "Ha Mim, they will not be helped.")

When this situation had lasted long for the Muslims, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to make peace with Uyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn Awf, the two chiefs of Ghatafan, on one third of the produce of Madinah, in return for them withdrawing with their people. Negotiations on this took place. He consulted the two Sa'ds about this. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if Allah has commanded you this, then we hear and obey. But if it is something you are doing for our sake, we have no need of it. We and these people were upon polytheism and the worship of idols, and they did not expect to eat any of its fruit except as hospitality or by purchase. Now that Allah has honoured us with Islam and guided us to it, and strengthened us through you, shall we give them our wealth? By Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword." So he approved their opinion and said: "This was only something I was doing for you, because I saw the Arabs had shot at you with a single bow."

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to Him belongs all praise, brought about a matter from His side by which He defeated the enemy, routed their hosts, and broke their strength. Among the means He prepared for this was that a man from Ghatafan, named Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud ibn Amir (may Allah be pleased with him), came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have embraced Islam, so command me as you wish." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are only one man, so cause discord among them on our behalf as far as you are able, for war is deception." He went at once to the Banu Qurayza, who had been his allies in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam). He entered upon them while they did not know of his conversion, and said: "O Banu Qurayza, you have fought Muhammad, and Quraysh, if they find an opportunity, will seize it; otherwise they will turn back to their own lands and leave you alone with Muhammad, who will then take his revenge on you." They said: "So what is to be done, O Nu'aym?" He said: "Do not fight alongside them until they give you hostages." They said: "You have given sound advice." Then he went on his way to Quraysh and said to them: "You know my affection for you and my sincere counsel to you." They said: "Yes." He said: "The Jews have regretted what they did in breaking their covenant with Muhammad and his companions, and they have sent word to him that they will take hostages from you and hand them over to him, and then they will side with him against you. So if they ask you for hostages, do not give them any." Then he went to Ghatafan and said to them the same thing.

When it was the night of Saturday in Shawwal, they sent to the Jews: "We are not a people who can remain in one place. The horses and the camels have perished, so rise up with us so that we may engage Muhammad." The Jews sent back to them: "Tomorrow is Saturday, and you know what befell those before us when they transgressed on it. Besides, we will not fight alongside you until you send us hostages."

When their messengers returned with this reply, Quraysh said: "Nu'aym has told you the truth, by Allah." They sent to the Jews: "By Allah, we will not send anyone to you. So come out with us until we engage Muhammad." Qurayza said: "Nu'aym has told you the truth, by Allah." Thus the two parties fell apart, and Allah sent against the polytheists a host of wind, which overturned their tents and left them no cooking pot without spilling it and no tent peg without uprooting it, so that they had no place of rest. And the host of Allah from the angels shook them and cast terror and fear into their hearts.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman to bring him news of them. He found them in this condition, already preparing to depart. He returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of the departure of the people. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found that Allah had turned back His enemy in their rage, having gained no good, and that Allah had spared him the fighting. He fulfilled His promise, strengthened His host, aided His servant, and defeated the confederates alone. The Messenger (ﷺ) entered Medina and laid down his weapons. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him while he was bathing in the house of Umm Salama and said: "Have you laid down your weapons? The angels have not yet laid down their weapons. Rise up to the expedition against these people," meaning the Banu Qurayza. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out:
"Whoever is listening and obeying, let him not pray the afternoon prayer except in the land of Banu Qurayza."
The Muslims set out swiftly. What happened to him and to the Banu Qurayza was as we have already mentioned. On the Day of the Trench and the Day of Qurayza, about ten of the Muslims were martyred.

[Section: The assassination of Abu Rafi' by Abdullah ibn Unays]

We have already mentioned that Abu Rafi' was among those who incited the confederates against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He was not killed along with the Banu Qurayza, as his companion Huyayy ibn Akhtab was killed. The Khazraj desired to kill him, to match the Aws in killing Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Allah, glorified and exalted, had made these two tribes vie with one another before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in good deeds. So they asked him for permission to kill him, and he granted it. Men from the Banu Salama were appointed for this, all of them from that clan: Abdullah ibn Atik, who was the leader of the group; Abdullah ibn Unays; Abu Qatada al-Harith ibn Rib'i; Mas'ud ibn Sinan; and Khuzaa'i ibn al-Aswad. They traveled until they reached him at Khaybar, in his house. They descended upon him at night, killed him, and returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Each of them claimed to have killed him. He said: "Show me your swords." When they showed him, he said of the sword of Abdullah ibn Unays: "This is the one that killed him; I see in it traces of food."

**(Benefit)**

When Messengers are sent to people, they are faced with one of two situations. Either one of them says, "I have believed," or he does not believe and remains in his misdeeds and disbelief. Both cases must be tested.

As for the one who says, "I have believed," his Lord will certainly test him and try him, so that it becomes clear whether he is truthful in his words, "I have believed," or a liar. If he is a liar, he turns back on his heels and flees the trial, just as he flees from the punishment of Allah. If he is truthful, he holds firm to his words, and the trial and testing only increase him in faith upon his faith. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly." And it increased them only in faith and submission.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22].

As for the one who does not believe, he will be tested in the Hereafter with punishment, and he will be afflicted by it, and this is the greater of the two trials. This is so if he is spared being tested by the punishment of this world and its calamities, and by its penalties which Allah inflicted upon those who did not follow His Messengers and disobeyed them. Therefore a trial is certain in this abode, in the barzakh (the intermediate realm), and on the Day of Resurrection for every person. But the believer's trial is lighter and his affliction easier, for Allah repels [harm] from him through faith, bears [some of his burden] for him because of it, and grants him patience, steadfastness, contentment and submission, by which his trial becomes easy for him.

As for the disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked, their trial and affliction are severe and lasting. So the trial of the believer is light and ends, while the trial of the disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked is severe and continuous.

Pain and trial are certain for every soul, whether it believes or disbelieves. But the believer experiences pain in this world at the outset, and then the outcome of both this world and the Hereafter is his. The disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked experience pleasure and bliss at the outset, and then they come to pain. So no one should hope to be entirely free of hardship and pain.

**(Section: On the mention of the fragrance of Paradise and the distance from which it is perceived)**

Al-Tabarani said: Musa ibn Hazim al-Asbahani narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Bukayr al-Hadrami narrated to us, Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah al-Fazari narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Amr, from Mujahid, from Junadah ibn Abi Umayyah, from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"Whoever kills a person from among the dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection) will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is perceived from a distance of one hundred years."

Al-Bukhari also narrated it in his Sahih, from Qays ibn Hafs, from Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Amr al-Fuqaymi, from Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr, without mentioning Junadah between them, and he said: "...is perceived from a distance of forty years."

Al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Sulayman, that is al-Basri, narrated to us, from Ibn Ajlan, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"Beware! Whoever kills a person under covenant (mu'ahad) who has the protection of Allah and His Messenger, has indeed broken the protection of Allah, and he will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is perceived from a distance of seventy autumns."

He said: "On this topic there is also a report from Abu Bakrah. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is hasan sahih (good and sound)." Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahid said: "Its isnad, in my view, meets the conditions of the sahih." I say: Al-Tabarani also narrated it from the hadith of Isa ibn Yunus, from Awf al-A'rabi, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever kills a person under covenant unjustly, will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, and the fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of one hundred years."

Al-Tabarani also said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, from Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan or another, from Abu Bakrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah say:

"The fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of one hundred years."

These wordings do not contradict one another in any way.

Both [al-Bukhari and Muslim] have also related in the two Sahihs (Sahihayn, the two authentic collections) from the hadith of Anas, who said: My uncle did not witness Badr with the Messenger of Allah. He said: "It grieved him." He said: "The first battle with the Messenger of Allah that I missed..." He said: "If Allah shows me another occasion to be with the Messenger of Allah, Allah will see what I do." He said: "So he feared to say anything other than that." He said: "Then he witnessed Uhud with the Messenger of Allah." He said: "Then he met Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and said to him, 'Where?' He said: 'Aha! By the fragrance of Paradise! I perceive it beyond Uhud.'" He said: "So he fought them until he was killed." He said: "He was found to have over eighty wounds on his body, from strikes, stabs and arrows." His sister, Amat al-Rubay' bint al-Nadr, said: "I did not recognise my brother except by his fingertips." And this verse was revealed: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted Allah upon.﴾ He said: "They used to think it was revealed concerning him and his companions."

The fragrance of Paradise is of two kinds. One is a fragrance found in this world, which souls sometimes smell, though people do not perceive it. The other is a fragrance perceived by the sense of smell of bodies, just as one smells the scents of flowers and other things. The people of Paradise share in perceiving this in the Hereafter, both near and far. In this world, it may be perceived by whomever Allah wills from among His prophets and messengers. What Anas ibn al-Nadr found may belong to either category, and Allah knows best.

Abu Nu'aym said: Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Mu'adhdhin narrated to us, Abd al-Wahid ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, al-Rabi' ibn Badr informed us, Harun ibn Riyab narrated to us, from Mujahid, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "The fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of five hundred years."

Al-Tabarani said: Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Hadrami narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Tarif narrated to us, my father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, Jabir al-Ju'fi related to me, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The fragrance of Paradise is perceived from a distance of a thousand years, and by Allah, an undutiful son and one who severs the ties of kinship will not smell it."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi said in his Musnad: Shu'bah narrated to us, from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever claims to be the son of someone other than his father will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is perceived from a distance of five hundred years. Allah, glorified is He, has indeed shown His servants in this abode some traces of Paradise and a sample of it: its pleasant fragrance, its desirable delights, its beautiful sights, its good fruits, its bliss, its joy, and the coolness of the eye."

**[Section: On the Battle of the Trench (Ghazwat al-Khandaq)]**

It took place in the fifth year after the Hijrah, in Shawwal, according to the more correct of the two opinions, since there is no dispute that the Battle of Uhud was in Shawwal of the third year. The polytheists had promised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a meeting in the following year, which was the fourth year, but then they broke their promise because of the drought of that year, and they returned. When the fifth year came, they came to fight him. This is the view of the people of the biographies and the military campaigns (Ahl al-Siyar wa al-Maghazi).

Musa ibn Uqbah differed with them and said: "Rather, it was in the fourth year." Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: "This is the correct view about which there is no doubt." He argued for it with the hadith of Ibn Umar in the Sahihayn, that he was presented to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud when he was fourteen years old, and he was not permitted [to fight]; then he was presented to him on the day of the Trench when he was fifteen years old, and he was permitted.

He said: "So it is established that there was only one year between them."

This was answered with two replies. The first: Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him back because he considered him too young for fighting, and permitted him when he reached the age at which he was seen to be capable. There is nothing in this that denies that the interval between them could have been a year or so.

The second: Perhaps the Battle of Uhud was at the beginning of his fourteenth year, and the Battle of the Trench at the end of his fifteenth year.

**[The cause of the Battle of the Trench]**

The cause of the Battle of the Trench was that when the Jews saw the victory of the polytheists over the Muslims at Uhud, and when they learned of Abu Sufyan's appointment to attack the Muslims, he went out for that purpose. Then he returned in the following year. The leaders of the Jews, such as Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Kinanah ibn al-Rabi' and others, went out to the Quraysh in Makkah to incite them to attack the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to stir them up against him, and they promised them on their own behalf to support them. The Quraysh responded to them. Then they went out to Ghatafan and called them, and they responded to them. Then they went around among the Arab tribes calling them to this, and whoever responded, responded. So the Quraysh went out, led by Abu Sufyan, with four thousand men. The Banu Sulaym joined them at Marr al-Zahran. The Banu Asad, Fazarah, Ashja' and Banu Murrah went out, and Ghatafan came with their leader Uyaynah ibn Hisn. The number of disbelievers who reached the Trench was ten thousand.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of their march against him, he consulted the Companions. Salman al-Farisi advised him to dig a trench which would stand between the enemy and Madinah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered it, and the Muslims hastened to it, and he himself worked in it. They also hastened to pre-empt the assault of the disbelievers against them. In the digging of the trench there were signs of his prophethood and marks of his messengership, of which the reports are widely transmitted. The digging of the Trench was in front of Sal', and Sal' is a mountain behind the backs of the Muslims, while the Trench lay between them and the disbelievers.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with three thousand Muslims. He was protected by the mountain at his back, and by the Trench in front of them.

Ibn Ishaq said: "He went out with seven hundred," but this is an error, derived from [the number who went out] at Uhud.

The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the women and children to be placed in the fortified towers of Madinah, and he appointed Ibn Umm Maktum as their deputy.

Huyayy ibn Akhtab set out to the Banu Qurayzah and approached their fortress. Ka'b ibn Asad refused to open it for him, but he kept speaking to him until he opened it for him. When he entered upon him, he said: "I have come to you with the honour of the age. I have come to you with the Quraysh, Ghatafan and Asad, under their commanders, to fight Muhammad." Ka'b said: "By Allah, you have come to me with the humiliation of the age, and with a cloud whose water has been poured out; it thunders and flashes, but there is nothing in it."

He kept at him until he broke the covenant between himself and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and joined the polytheists in fighting him. The polytheists rejoiced at this. Ka'b stipulated with Huyayy that if they did not overcome Muhammad, he would come and enter his fortress with him, and suffer what he suffered. Huyayy agreed to this and fulfilled it to him.

News of the Banu Qurayzah and their breaking of the covenant reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he sent to them al-Sa'dayn (Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn Ubadah), Khawwat ibn Jubayr, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah, to find out whether they were still upholding their covenant or had broken it. When they drew near to them, they found them in the worst condition: they openly reviled them with abuse and hostility, and they insulted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So they withdrew from them and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) using indirect words to inform him that they had broken the covenant and acted treacherously. This was grievous to the Muslims. At that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Allahu Akbar! Rejoice, O assembly of Muslims!"

The trial intensified, hypocrisy appeared, and some of the Banu Harithah asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to go back to Madinah, saying: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed, though they were not exposed. They only intended to flee.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13].

The Banu Salamah were inclined to cowardice, but then Allah made both groups firm.

The polytheists remained besieging the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a month, and there was no fighting between them, because of what Allah had placed of the Trench between them and the Muslims, except that some horsemen of the Quraysh, among them Amr ibn Abd Wudd and a group with him, came towards the Trench. When they stood at it, they said: "This is a stratagem which the Arabs did not know." Then they aimed for a narrow place in the Trench, forced their way across it, and their horses roamed in the salt flat between the Trench and Sal'. They called for single combat, and Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) volunteered for Amr. He fought him, and Allah killed him at his hands. He had been one of the bravest and champions of the polytheists. The rest fled back to their companions. (The war-cry of the Muslims that day was: "Ha Mim, they will not be helped.")

When this situation had lasted long for the Muslims, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to make peace with Uyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn Awf, the two chiefs of Ghatafan, on one third of the produce of Madinah, in return for them withdrawing with their people. Negotiations on this took place. He consulted the two Sa'ds about this. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if Allah has commanded you this, then we hear and obey. But if it is something you are doing for our sake, we have no need of it. We and these people were upon polytheism and the worship of idols, and they did not expect to eat any of its fruit except as hospitality or by purchase. Now that Allah has honoured us with Islam and guided us to it, and strengthened us through you, shall we give them our wealth? By Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword." So he approved their opinion and said: "This was only something I was doing for you, because I saw the Arabs had shot at you with a single bow."

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to Him belongs all praise, brought about a matter from His side by which He defeated the enemy, routed their hosts, and broke their strength. Among the means He prepared for this was that a man from Ghatafan, named Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud ibn Amir (may Allah be pleased with him), came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have embraced Islam, so command me as you wish." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are only one man, so cause discord among them on our behalf as far as you are able, for war is deception." He went at once to the Banu Qurayza, who had been his allies in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam). He entered upon them while they did not know of his conversion, and said: "O Banu Qurayza, you have fought Muhammad, and Quraysh, if they find an opportunity, will seize it; otherwise they will turn back to their own lands and leave you alone with Muhammad, who will then take his revenge on you." They said: "So what is to be done, O Nu'aym?" He said: "Do not fight alongside them until they give you hostages." They said: "You have given sound advice." Then he went on his way to Quraysh and said to them: "You know my affection for you and my sincere counsel to you." They said: "Yes." He said: "The Jews have regretted what they did in breaking their covenant with Muhammad and his companions, and they have sent word to him that they will take hostages from you and hand them over to him, and then they will side with him against you. So if they ask you for hostages, do not give them any." Then he went to Ghatafan and said to them the same thing.

When it was the night of Saturday in Shawwal, they sent to the Jews: "We are not a people who can remain in one place. The horses and the camels have perished, so rise up with us so that we may engage Muhammad." The Jews sent back to them: "Tomorrow is Saturday, and you know what befell those before us when they transgressed on it. Besides, we will not fight alongside you until you send us hostages."

When their messengers returned with this reply, Quraysh said: "Nu'aym has told you the truth, by Allah." They sent to the Jews: "By Allah, we will not send anyone to you. So come out with us until we engage Muhammad." Qurayza said: "Nu'aym has told you the truth, by Allah." Thus the two parties fell apart, and Allah sent against the polytheists a host of wind, which overturned their tents and left them no cooking pot without spilling it and no tent peg without uprooting it, so that they had no place of rest. And the host of Allah from the angels shook them and cast terror and fear into their hearts.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman to bring him news of them. He found them in this condition, already preparing to depart. He returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of the departure of the people. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found that Allah had turned back His enemy in their rage, having gained no good, and that Allah had spared him the fighting. He fulfilled His promise, strengthened His host, aided His servant, and defeated the confederates alone. The Messenger (ﷺ) entered Medina and laid down his weapons. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him while he was bathing in the house of Umm Salama and said: "Have you laid down your weapons? The angels have not yet laid down their weapons. Rise up to the expedition against these people," meaning the Banu Qurayza. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out:
"Whoever is listening and obeying, let him not pray the afternoon prayer except in the land of Banu Qurayza."
The Muslims set out swiftly. What happened to him and to the Banu Qurayza was as we have already mentioned. On the Day of the Trench and the Day of Qurayza, about ten of the Muslims were martyred.
