The fact that the 'iddah (waiting period) is a right of the husband is indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then you have no waiting period from them that you should count﴾. So His saying: ﴿then you have no waiting period from them﴾ is evidence that the 'iddah is owed by the woman to the man.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 33, verse 50:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her, [she is] exclusively yours, not [for] the believers﴾

It is possible that the giving (al-hibah) is the conditional clause (shart), and the act of wishing (al-iradah) is its response (jawab). The meaning would then be: if she gives herself to the Prophet, then if the Prophet wishes to marry her, she is exclusively his.

It is also possible that the wishing is the conditional clause and the giving is its response. The meaning would then be: if the Prophet wishes to marry her, then if she gives herself, she is exclusively his.

Both possibilities are admitted. And God knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 33, verse 56 (part 1 of 9):

Mahmud ibn Khidash narrated to us: Jarir informed us, from Mughira, from Abu Ma'shar, from Ibrahim, who said: They said, "O Messenger of Allah, we already know how to greet you with peace (al-salam), so how should we send blessings upon you (al-salah)?" He said: "Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, Your servant and Your Messenger, and upon his family, as You sent blessings upon the family of Ibrahim. Indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us: al-Sari ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Hasan say:
"When the verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace in abundance﴾, they said, "O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace, we already know how it is. So how are we commanded to send blessings upon you?" He said: "Say: O Allah, make Your blessings and Your mercy upon the family of Muhammad as You made them upon the family of Ibrahim. Indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.""

Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us: Amr ibn Musafir narrated to us: a shaykh from my people narrated to me, saying: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say:
"No supplication is ever left without the Prophet (ﷺ) being blessed before it, except that it remains suspended between the heaven and the earth."

In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, from Abu Qurra al-Asadi, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:
"Indeed, supplication is held suspended between the heaven and the earth; nothing of it ascends until you send blessings upon your Prophet (ﷺ)."
It has also been narrated as a marfu' report, but the mawquf (halted) version is more sound.

(Section)
Ibn al-Qayyim said in Badai' al-Fawa'id:
As for the twenty-fourth question, which is: what is the wisdom in emphasizing the command to greet the Prophet (ﷺ) with the verbal noun, but not the blessing upon him, in His saying: ﴿Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace in abundance﴾?
Its answer is: the emphasis falls upon both the blessing and the greeting, though the direction of emphasis differs. At the beginning of the verse He, glorified is He, informed of His blessing upon him and the blessing of His angels upon him, emphasizing this information with the particle "inna" and informing about the angels with a plural noun in the genitive, which conveys generality and comprehensiveness. When souls sense that his station with Allah and with His angels is this station, they hasten to send blessings upon him, even if they are not commanded to do so; it is enough to alert them and point to it with the slightest indication. When they are commanded to it, they do not need the command to be emphasized; rather, when a bare command comes, they hasten and rush to agree with Allah and His angels in blessing him, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. Thus the act did not need to be emphasized by a verbal noun. But since the greeting was free of this meaning and came in the scope of a bare command rather than a report, its emphasis by the verbal noun is fitting, to indicate the realization and affirmation of the meaning. The emphasis of the verb takes the place of its repetition, just as repetition occurred in the blessing, both as report and as demand; so too honor occurred in the greeting, both as verb and as verbal noun. So reflect upon it.
For it is most wondrous. And Allah knows best. We have mentioned some of the secrets and wondrous wisdoms of this verse in the book "Ta'zim Sha'n al-Salah wa al-Salam ala Khayr al-Anam," and we brought therein benefits that equal at least a journey's worth of what is not found elsewhere, and to Allah belongs praise. So we limit ourselves here to this one point.

(Section)
As for the twenty-fifth question, which is: what is the wisdom in placing the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) before the blessing in the prayer, and why did the beginning not follow what Allah began with in the verse?
This too is a question of significance that should not be dismissed lightly or passed over. The Prophet (ﷺ) was extremely careful to follow the order that Allah set and to begin with what He began with. Thus he began with al-Safa in the sa'i and said: "We begin with what Allah began with" (sahih). He began with the face, then the hands, then the head in wudu', and he did not neglect this in a single instance; rather this was his wudu' until he departed this world, and he would put last what was to be last and never put first what was to be last. No one can transmit from him any contrary practice, neither with a sound chain, nor a good one, nor a weak one. Yet despite this, in the blessing and greeting upon him, the greeting was placed before the blessing. This is for a secret of the prayer, which we indicate briefly as the situation allows: the prayer comprises the servitude of all the limbs and organs together with the servitude of the heart, so each organ has a share of servitude. All the members and limbs of the worshipper move in the prayer as servitude to God, humility and submission. When the worshipper completes this servitude and his movements end, he concludes with sitting before the Lord, exalted is He, a sitting of abasement, brokenness and submission to His greatness, glorified is He, as a humble servant sits before his master. The sitting of prayer is the most humble of sittings and the greatest in submission and abasement. So in this state the servant is permitted to praise Allah, blessed and exalted is He, with the most eloquent kinds of praise, which is "at-tahiyyat lillah, as-salawat, at-tayyibat" (all greetings, prayers and good things are for Allah). It was their custom, when they entered upon their kings, to greet them in a manner befitting them, and that greeting is an honoring of them and praise of them; and Allah is more worthy of honor and praise than any of His creatures. So in His saying "at-tahiyyat, as-salawat, at-tayyibat" the servant gathers all kinds of praise of Allah, and affirms that these belong to Him by way of attribute and dominion. Likewise, all prayers are for Allah: it is He alone to whom prayer is offered, not another. Likewise all good things, words and deeds, are His: His words are good, His deeds are good, and He is Good, and none ascends to Him but the good, and "to Him ascends the good word" (Qur'an 35:10). So all good things are His and from Him and toward Him: they are His by dominion and attribute, from Him is their coming and beginning, and to Him is their ascent and end. The prayer comprises righteous deeds and good words, and "the good word ascends to Him, and righteous deed raises it" (Qur'an 35:10). So it is fitting to mention this at the end of the prayer, at the time of its ascent to Allah, the Exalted. Then the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) follows: when he has brought this praise of the Lord, he turns to the status of the Messenger through whom this good came to be, and greets him with the most complete greeting, defined with the article "al" that denotes totality, joined with mercy and blessing. This is the most authentic formula of greeting upon him, so do not be stingy with the article "al" in this station. Then he moves to greeting himself and all the righteous servants of Allah, beginning with himself, for it is more important, and a person begins with himself and then with those he supports. Then he concludes this station with the bond of Islam, which is the testimony of the truth, the testimony that is the first and last of the matter, and in which all praise is contained. Then he moves to another kind, which is supplication and request. The tashahhud thus combines two kinds of supplication: the supplication of praise and good, and the supplication of request and asking. The first is the nobler of the two, for it is the right of the Lord and His attribute, while the second is the servant's portion and benefit. A narration says: "Whoever is occupied with My remembrance rather than asking Me, I give him the best of what I give to those who ask" (weak).
But since the prayer is the most complete of acts of worship in servitude and the most perfect, both kinds are prescribed in it, and the first is put forward for its excellence. Then he moves to the second kind, the supplication of request and asking, and begins with its most important, most majestic and most beneficial part for the servant, which is asking Allah, exalted is He, for blessing upon His Messenger (ﷺ). This is among the most excellent supplications of the servant and the most beneficial for him in this world and the next, as we have mentioned in the book "Ta'zim Sha'n al-Salah ala al-Nabi." It also contains the point that the supplicant places it as a preface before his need and his request for himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated this meaning in his saying: "Then let him choose from the supplication whatever pleases him." Likewise in the hadith of Fadala ibn Ubayd: "When one of you supplicates, let him begin with praising Allah and extolling Him, then let him send blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then let him supplicate." So reflect how the tashahhud, from its beginning to its end, came in conformity with this and arranged in the finest order. The hadith of Fadala is what has disclosed and clarified and explained this meaning for us. So may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, through whom He completed our religion for us, perfected His favor upon us by his message, and made him a mercy to the worlds and a grief to the disbelievers.

(Section)
As for the twenty-sixth question, which is: what is the wisdom in the greeting being in the second person address while the blessing is in the third person?
Its answer becomes apparent from what preceded. The blessing upon him is a request and asking from Allah that He bless him, so only the third person form is possible in it, since one does not say "O Allah, bless you." As for greeting him, it is in the form of the present addressee, treating him as one face to face, for a most wondrous wisdom: when he (ﷺ) was dearer to the believer than his own self between his two sides, more fitting for him and closer, and his mental reality and his knowledgeable likeness were present in his heart such that nothing of him is absent except his physical person, as the poet said:
"Your image is in my eyes, your remembrance is on my tongue,
And your dwelling is in my heart, so where could you be absent?"
Whoever is in this state is truly present, and another, even if physically present to the eyes, is absent from the heart. So his address was the address of confrontation and presence, and greeting him with the second person is more fitting than greeting in the third person, treating him as one face to face and seen, because of his nearness to the heart and his indwelling in all its parts, such that no part of the heart remains without his love and remembrance in it, as it is said:
"If my heart were split open, you would see your remembrance at its center."
The unity in the line "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" is not to be thought strange: the beloved's dominion over the lover's heart and his overpowering of it, so that it is as if he sees him. For this reason you find them, in addressing their beloved, relying on the address of presence and witnessing, despite the great physical distance, because of the perfection of spiritual nearness. Bodily distance did not prevent them from conversing with spirits and addressing them. Whoever's nature is coarse is far removed from all this. Love may reach among its people to the point that one sees his beloved in nearness to him as in the position of his soul, nothing being closer to him than it, as it is said:
"O you who dwell in my breast and my inner heart, though his dwellings are far from me."
And love may refine its state so that one sees it as closer to him and nearer than his soul, and these verses touch on this:
"He is closer to the lover than his own self, though he is far from his eye,
And whoever has such love, how could he become forgetful of it?"
Then it refines its state and subdues its authority until the lover, through his beloved, is absent from himself, so that he feels only his beloved and does not feel himself. From here arose the Sufi ecstatic utterances (shathahat), whose source is the strength of the inspiration and the weakness of discernment. Its holder judges by the state over knowledge and makes the state the arbiter and removes his knowledge from between. Those who are protected in this matter judge that the ruling of knowledge governs the authority of the state, and they know that every state over which knowledge does not rule should not be trusted or relied upon, except as one relies upon the overpowered and subdued in what overtakes him and he cannot repel. This is the condition of the perfected among the people, who combined the light of knowledge with states of practice; the storms of their states did not extinguish the light of their knowledge, nor did their knowledge fall short of their advancement to what lies beyond it of the stations of faith and excellence. These are the judges over both groups. As for others, they are either veiled by a knowledge that has no authority over them, or deceived by a state without knowledge of its sound from its corrupt. And Allah, exalted is He, is asked for His bounty; He is near and responsive. The perfected one is he who lets knowledge rule over the state, so he manages his state by his knowledge and makes knowledge like the light by which he distinguishes the sound from the corrupt, not one who discredits knowledge in favor of the state and makes the state the standard and balance for it: whatever agrees with his state from knowledge he accepts, and whatever contradicts it he rejects and negates. This is the root of error in this domain. Rather, the obligation is to make knowledge the judge and to return to its rule. On this the gnostic shaykhs of the path all advised and urged the strongest urging upon knowledge, because of their awareness of the perils and ruins contained in the bare state without it: "And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path" (Qur'an 2:213).

(Section: On the explanation of the meaning of prayer (salah) upon the Prophet (ﷺ))
The root of this word in the language returns to two meanings:
The first: supplication and blessing.
The second: worship. From the first is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them; indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ (9:103).
And His saying, exalted is He, concerning the hypocrites: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave﴾ (9:84).
And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If one of you is invited to a meal, let him accept; if he is fasting, let him pray." Both interpretations have been given: it was said, let him supplicate for them with blessing; and it was said, let him pray (perform prayer) there in place of eating. It was also said that salah in the language means supplication.
Supplication is of two kinds: supplication of worship and supplication of request. The worshipper is a supplicant just as the petitioner is a supplicant, and both are the meanings of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ (40:60). It was said: obey Me, I will reward you; and it was said: ask Me, I will give to you. And both meanings were given for His saying: ﴿When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ (2:186).
The correct view is that supplication encompasses both kinds, and this is a univocal term, not a homonym. Its use for the supplication of worship includes His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides Allah; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on earth﴾ (34:22), and His saying: ﴿And those who call upon besides Allah create nothing, while they are created﴾ (16:20).
And His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾ (25:77). The sounder of the two views is: were it not that you call upon Him and worship Him; that is, what would He care for you were it not for your worship of Him? So the verbal noun is here an object of the agent.
And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly; indeed He does not love transgressors. And do not corrupt the earth after its reformation, and call upon Him in fear and hope﴾ (7:55–56). And He, exalted is He, said, reporting about His prophets and messengers: ﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in desire and fear﴾ (21:90).
This approach is better than the first, and the claim of disagreement over the referent of supplication disappears, and with it the problems raised about the name "salah" in the sacred law: whether it is transferred from its place in the language, making it a technical sacred meaning (haqiqa shar'iyya), or a sacred metaphor (majaz shar'i).
On this basis, salah remains upon its linguistic referent, which is supplication. Supplication is of worship and of request, and the one praying from his takbir to his salam is between supplication of worship and supplication of request. So he is in a real salah, neither metaphorical nor transferred. But the name "salah" was specified for this particular worship, as with other words which the people of language and custom restrict to some part of their referent, such as "dabba" (beast) and "ra's" (head) and the like. This is at most a specification and restriction of the word to part of its original meaning, and therefore it does not entail transfer or departure from its original meaning. And Allah knows best.

(Section)
This is the prayer of the human being. As for Allah's blessing upon His servant, it is of two kinds: general and special.
The general is His blessing upon His believing servants, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who blesses you, and His angels [do so]﴾ (33:43).
And from this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication of blessing upon individual believers, such as his saying: "O Allah, bless the family of Abu Awfa." In another hadith, a woman said to him: "Bless me and my husband," and he said: "May Allah bless you and your husband." This hadith and what resembles it will be mentioned, Allah willing.
The second kind is His special blessing upon His prophets and messengers, especially upon the seal of them and the best of them, Muhammad (ﷺ).
People have differed about the meaning of Allah's blessing upon him, in several views:
The first: that it is His mercy. Isma'il narrated to us: Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Sawa' narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: "The blessing of Allah is His mercy, and the blessing of the angels is supplication." [Its chain is weak.]
Al-Mubarrad said: the root of salah is the womb (rahim), so from Allah it is mercy, and from the angels it is tenderness and a request for mercy from Allah. This view is the well-known one among many later scholars.
The second view: that the blessing of Allah is His forgiveness. Isma'il narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Sawa' narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, concerning His saying "He it is who blesses you": "The blessing of Allah is His forgiveness, and the blessing of the angels is supplication." [Very weak.]

This statement belongs to the same category as the one before it, and both are weak, for several reasons.

First, Allah, glorified is He, distinguished between His prayers (ṣalawāt) upon His servants and His mercy (raḥmah), saying, ﴿And give good tidings to the patient, who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return." Those are the ones upon whom are blessings (ṣalawāt) from their Lord and mercy, and those are the rightly guided.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 157]. He joined mercy to prayers with the conjunction (ʿaṭf), which requires that the two be different. This is the basic principle of conjunction.

As for their saying, "(And he found her saying a lie and a sin...)" [a line of poetry], it is an anomalous and rare usage, and the most eloquent speech is not interpreted in accordance with it. Moreover, *al-may(n)* (a lie made to bind) is more specific than *al-kadhib* (lying).

The second reason is that Allah's prayer is specific to His prophets, messengers and believing servants, whereas His mercy encompasses everything. Therefore prayer is not synonymous with mercy. Rather, mercy is among the necessary results (lawāzim), consequences and fruits of prayer. Whoever explains it as mercy has explained it by part of its fruit and purpose. This occurs often in the explanation of the words of the Qur'an, and the Messenger (ﷺ) would explain a word by its necessary concomitant and part of its meaning, such as explaining *al-rayb* (doubt) as *al-shakk* (uncertainty), and *al-shakk* is part of the meaning of *al-rayb*; explaining *al-maghfirah* (forgiveness) as *al-sitr* (covering), which is part of the meaning of *al-maghfirah*; and explaining *al-raḥmah* (mercy) as the desire for goodness (*irādat al-iḥsān*), which is a necessary concomitant of mercy. Examples of this are numerous, and we have mentioned them in the principles of tafsir.

The third reason is that there is no disagreement about the permissibility of asking for mercy for the believers, whereas the early and later scholars differed on the permissibility of sending prayers upon the prophets, in three positions which we will mention later, if Allah wills. It is therefore known that the two are not synonymous.

The fourth reason is that if prayer meant mercy, it would fulfil the command in place of mercy, and it would remove the obligation according to those who make it obligatory, if one says, "O Allah, have mercy upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad." But the matter is not so.

The fifth reason is that one does not say of someone who showed mercy to another, and was tender towards him, and fed him, gave him drink or clothed him, that he prayed for him (ṣallā ʿalayhi), but one says that he has shown him mercy (raḥimahu).

The sixth reason is that a person may show mercy to someone he hates and is hostile towards, finding mercy in his heart for him, and yet he does not pray for him.

The seventh reason is that prayer must necessarily contain speech. It is praise (thanāʾ) from the one who prays upon the one for whom he prays, and an honouring (tanwīh) of him, an indication of his virtues and merits, and a mention of him.

Al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, who said: "The prayer of Allah upon His Messenger is His praise of him in the presence of the angels." [[Its chain is capable of being upgraded to acceptable (qābil lil-taḥassun).]]

Ismāʿīl also said in his book: Naṣr ibn ʿAlī narrated to us: Khālid ibn Yazīd narrated to us, from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, concerning ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send prayers upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 56]: he said, "The prayer of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is His praise of him, and the prayer of the angels upon him is supplication (duʿāʾ)."

The eighth reason is that Allah, glorified is He, distinguished between His prayer and the prayer of His angels, and combined them in one act, saying, ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send prayers upon the Prophet﴾. This prayer cannot be mercy; rather, it is His praise, glorified is He, and the praise of His angels upon him. It is not said that *al-ṣalāh* is a shared term (lafẓ mushtarak), and that it may be used in both of its meanings together, because there are numerous objections to that:

The first is that homonymy (ishtirāk) is contrary to the original principle. Indeed, it is not known that it occurred in the language from a single coiner, as the linguists, among them al-Mubarrad and others, have stated explicitly. Rather, it occurs by accident, by chance, because of the plurality of coiners; then the language becomes mixed, and homonymy results.

The second is that the majority do not permit using a homonymous term in both its meanings, neither literally (ḥaqīqah) nor figuratively (majāz). What is reported from al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding his permitting this, is not authentic from him. It arose from his saying that if one bequeaths to his *mawālī* (clients/freed slaves, or masters) and he has *mawālī* above and below him, all of them are included. Someone thought that the word *mawlā* is a homonym covering both, and that when used without qualification it is understood as both. This is not correct, for the word *mawlā* is one of the univocal (mutawāṭiʾ) terms; al-Shāfiʿī, according to the apparent position of his school, and Aḥmad, both hold that both categories of *mawālī* enter into this term, and it is according to him a general (ʿāmm) univocal term, not a homonym.

As for what is reported from al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said in a discussion concerning ﴿or you have touched women﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 43], when it was said to him that *al-mulāmasah* may mean intercourse, he said: "It is to be understood literally as touching with the hand, and figuratively as intercourse." This is not authentic from al-Shāfiʿī, nor is it of the kind of his familiar speech; rather, it is from the speech of some later jurists. We have mentioned, in refuting the use of a homonymous term in both its meanings together, some fifteen proofs in the issue of *al-qurʾ* (the term for menstrual period/purity) in our book *al-Taʿlīq ʿalā al-Aḥkām*.

So if the meaning of *al-ṣalāh* is praise of the Messenger, care for him, and manifestation of his nobility, virtue and sanctity, as is well known of this word, then the word *al-ṣalāh* in the verse is not a homonym to be understood in both its meanings. Rather, it may be used in one meaning, and this is the original principle. We will return to this issue, if Allah wills, in the discussion of the explanation of His words, ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send prayers upon the Prophet﴾.

The ninth reason is that Allah, glorified is He, commanded the prayer upon him immediately after informing that He and His angels send prayers upon him. The meaning is: since Allah and His angels send prayers upon His Messenger, then you too send prayers upon him; you are more worthy to send prayers upon him and to greet him with peace (taslīm) for what you have attained through the blessing of his messengership and the favour of his mission (safārah), of the nobility of this world and the Hereafter. It is known that if this meaning were expressed by mercy, its placement would not be fitting, and the wording would not be fine, so the wording and the meaning would be confounded. The sense would become: "Allah and His angels show mercy and ask forgiveness for His Prophet, so you too invoke for him and greet him." This is certainly not what the verse intends. Rather, the prayer commanded therein is the request from Allah of what He informed of concerning His prayer and the prayer of His angels, and it is praise of him, manifestation of his virtue and nobility, and the will to honour him and bring him near. It therefore includes both information and request. This supplication and invocation from us is called prayer upon him for two reasons:

The first is that it includes the praiser's praise of him, the proclaiming of his nobility and virtue, and the will and love for this from Allah, the Exalted. Thus it includes both information and request.

The second reason is that it is called prayer from us because we ask Allah to send prayers upon him. So Allah's prayer upon him is His praise and His will to raise his mention and bring him near, and our prayer upon him is our request of Allah, the Exalted, that He do this for him. The opposite of this is the cursing (laʿnah) of his enemies who hate what he brought. It is attributed both to Allah and to the servant, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed those who conceal what We sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear to the people in the Book, those—Allah curses them, and the cursers curse them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 159]. Allah's cursing of them includes His condemnation of them, His distancing of them, and His hatred of them; the servant's cursing includes his request of Allah, the Exalted, that He do this to one who deserves His curse.

When this is established, it is known that if prayer were mercy, it would not be correct to say of one who requests it from Allah that he is "one who prays" (muṣallī); rather, one would say he is "one who seeks mercy for him" (mustarḥim lahu), just as one who asks for forgiveness is called "one who seeks forgiveness for him" (mustaghfir lahu), and one who asks for kindness is called "one who seeks kindness for him" (mustaʿṭif), and similar terms.

For this reason one does not say of one who asked Allah for forgiveness for another, "He has forgiven him, so he is a forgiver," nor of one who asked Allah to pardon someone, "He has pardoned him." Here, however, the servant is named one who prays (muṣallī). So if prayer were mercy, the servant would be a merciful one towards whoever he prays for, and he would have shown him mercy; and whoever shows mercy to the Prophet (ﷺ) once, Allah shows mercy to him ten times. This is clearly false.

If it is said that the meaning of the servant's prayer upon him (ﷺ) is not his showing mercy, but rather his request of mercy for him from Allah, it is answered: this is false for several reasons.

The first is that seeking mercy is required for every Muslim, whereas seeking prayer from Allah is specific to His messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, according to many people, as we will mention, if Allah wills.

The second is that if one who seeks mercy were named one who prays, then one who seeks forgiveness would be named a forgiver, one who seeks pardon would be named a pardoner, one who seeks pardon for sins would be named a pardoner (ṣāfiḥ), and similar.

If it is said: "You too have named one who seeks prayer from Allah a one who prays," it is answered: he is named one who prays because the reality of prayer exists in him, for its reality is praise, the will for honour and nearness, and the elevation of rank; and this is present in the servant's prayer. But the servant wills this from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Allah, glorified and exalted is He, wills it from Himself, that He do it for His Messenger (ﷺ).

As for the second answer, that he is named one who prays because of his request of this from Allah, this is because prayer is a kind of speech, requestive and informative (khabarī), and the will is present in it; this is found in the one who prays, unlike mercy and forgiveness, which are acts that do not come about from the one who asks, but come about from the one who is asked. And Allah knows best.

The tenth reason is that it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ), in the authentic ḥadīth narrated by Muslim, that whoever sends one prayer upon him, Allah sends ten prayers upon him in return; and that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said to him: "Whoever of your community sends one prayer upon you, I send ten prayers upon him." This agrees with the established principle in the Sharīʿah that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. So Allah's prayer upon the one who prays upon His Messenger is a recompense for his prayer upon him. It is known that the servant's prayer upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is not mercy from the servant, such that Allah's prayer upon him would be of its kind; rather, it is praise of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the will of Allah, the Exalted, that He raise his mention and increase him in honour and nobility. The recompense is of the same kind as the deed: whoever praises the Messenger (ﷺ), Allah rewards him in kind by praising him and increasing his honour and dignity. Thus the link of the recompense to the deed is valid, and its conformity to it and suitability for it are sound, like His saying: "Whoever eases a debtor in difficulty, Allah eases him in this world and the Hereafter; whoever covers a Muslim, Allah covers him in this world and the Hereafter; whoever relieves a believer of a distress of the distresses of this world, Allah relieves him of a distress of the distresses of the Day of Resurrection; Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother; and whoever takes a path seeking knowledge therein, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise."

And whoever is asked about a knowledge he has and conceals it will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire. [[This is a ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth.]]

And whoever sends one prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ), Allah sends ten prayers upon him in return, and the similar examples are numerous.

The eleventh reason is that if someone said, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may Allah have mercy on him," or said, "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah have mercy on him," in place of (ﷺ), the community would hasten to denounce him, and would name him an innovator, one who does not revere the Prophet (ﷺ), nor sends prayers upon him, nor praises him in the manner he deserves, and who does not deserve that Allah send ten prayers upon him for that. And if Allah's prayer were mercy, nothing of that would be prohibited.

The twelfth reason is that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among yourselves like the call of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nūr: 63]. He, glorified is He, thus commanded that His Messenger not be called in the manner people call one another; rather, one says, "O Messenger of Allah," and does not say, "O Muhammad." He would be addressed by his name at the time of addressing the disbelievers, whereas the Muslims would address him as "O Messenger of Allah." If this is so in addressing him, then likewise in his absence: one should not make what is invoked for him of the kind of what we invoke for one another; rather, he should be invoked for with the noblest invocation, which is prayer upon him. It is known that mercy is invoked for every Muslim, and even for non-human animals, as in the prayer for rain: "O Allah, have mercy upon Your servants, Your lands and Your livestock."

The thirteenth reason is that this expression is not known in the original language with the meaning of mercy at all. What is known among the Arabs of its meaning is supplication (duʿāʾ), blessing (tabrīk) and praise (thanāʾ). One says,

"(And if you mention her, he prayed upon her, and Zamzam...)" [a line of poetry]

that is, he blessed her and praised her. The Arabs never used *ṣallā ʿalayhi* in the sense of mercy. Therefore it is obligatory to interpret the word according to its meaning as customary in the language.

The fourteenth reason is that it is permissible, and even recommended, for everyone to ask Allah, the Exalted, to have mercy upon him, so he says, "O Allah, have mercy upon me." As the Prophet (ﷺ) taught the one who supplicated to say, "O Allah, forgive me, have mercy upon me, grant me well-being and provide for me," and when he memorised it he said, "As for this, he has filled his hands with good." It is known that it is not permissible for anyone to say, "O Allah, send prayers upon me," rather, the one who invokes thus is transgressing in his supplication: ﴿and Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 55].

Unlike asking for mercy, for Allah, the Exalted, loves that His servant ask Him for forgiveness and mercy. So it is known that their meaning is not one.

The fifteenth reason is that most of the contexts in which mercy is used are not fitting for prayer to be used in them. Such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 156]; and His saying, "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath"; and His saying: ﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 56]; and His saying: ﴿And He is merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 43]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed He is kind and merciful to them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117]; and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Allah is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child"; and his saying, "Show mercy to those on the earth, and the One in heaven will show mercy to you" [[This is a ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth.]]; and his saying, "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy"; and his saying, "Mercy is not removed except from a wretch" [[Its chain is ḥasan.]]; and his saying, "As for the sheep, if you show it mercy, Allah will show you mercy" [[Its isnād is ṣaḥīḥ.]]. So the contexts in which mercy is used with respect to Allah and to the servants are such that prayer would not be fitting in many of them, indeed in most of them. Therefore, explaining prayer as mercy is not correct. And Allah knows best.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said concerning ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send prayers upon the Prophet﴾: "They bless him." This does not contradict explaining it as praise and the will for honour and magnification, for blessing from Allah includes that. That is why He joined the prayer upon him with the blessing upon him. And the angels said to Ibrāhīm: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾ [Hūd: 73]; and the Messiah said: ﴿And He made me blessed wherever I am﴾ [Maryam: 31].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 33, verse 56 (part 3 of 9):

Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: "[The meaning of 'mubarak' is] one who teaches goodness wherever he is." This is a part of its meaning. The one who is blessed (mubarak) is abundant in goodness within himself, which he conveys to others through teaching, enabling, advising, willing (good for them), and striving. For this reason a servant is "mubarak" because Allah has blessed him and made him so. And Allah, exalted is He, is "mutabarik" (blessed/exalted in blessing) because all blessing comes from Him. So His servant is blessed, and He is the Blessed One. ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. And His saying ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is Able over all things﴾.

We will return to this meaning shortly, if Allah wills.

Some people have rejected the interpretation of prayer (salah) from Allah as mercy (rahmah), saying that rahmah means tenderness of nature (ruqqat al-tab'), which is impossible with respect to Allah, exalted is He, just as supplication (du'a') from Him is impossible.

What he said is a trace of the Jahmi tendency, which seeps from his heart onto his tongue. Its reality is the outright denial of Allah's mercy altogether. Jahm used to go out to the lepers and say, "The Most Merciful of the merciful," doing this as a denial of His mercy, exalted is He.

What this speaker supposed is the doubt of those who deny the attributes of the Lord, exalted is He. They said: will (irade) is the movement of the soul to bring what benefits it and to repel what harms it, and the Lord, exalted above that, has no will. Anger (ghadab) is the boiling of the blood of the heart seeking revenge, and the Lord is free of that, so He has no anger. They followed this false path in His life, His speech, and all His attributes. This is among the most false of falsehoods, for it takes the specific characteristics of the created as the definition of the attribute, then negates it entirely from the Creator. This is in the extreme of deception and misleading. For the specific feature they took from the attribute is not established for it in itself; rather it is established only by its attachment to a possible created being. It is known that negating the specific features of the attributes of created beings from the Creator does not entail negating the basic attribute from Him, and affirming the basic attribute for Him does not entail affirming the specific features of the created for Him. Likewise, what is negated from the attributes of the Lord, exalted is He, of deficiencies and resemblance to creation does not entail negating it from the attributes of the created; nor does what is established for them of necessity, eternity and perfection entail its establishment for the created; nor does applying the attribute to both the Creator and the created. This is like life and knowledge. The life of a servant is subject to afflictions opposed to it, such as sickness, sleep and death; and likewise his knowledge is subject to forgetfulness and ignorance opposed to it. This is impossible for the life and knowledge of the Lord. Whoever negates the knowledge and life of the Lord because of what befalls them in the created has erred. It is the parallel of one who negates the mercy of the Lord, or His knowledge, because of the tenderness of nature that befalls mercy in the created, and the supposition of one who imagines that knowledge, life or will cannot be conceived except with the specific features of the created.

The source of this error is nothing but imagining the attribute of the created as bound to it first, and imagining that affirming it for Allah is with this same restriction. These are two false illusions. For the attribute established for Allah is attached to Him, and no feature of the created can be imagined in it, neither in its wording nor in the establishment of its meaning. Whoever negates from the Lord, exalted is He, any of His attributes on account of this false imagining is obliged to negate all the attributes of His perfection, since he can only conceive of them as the attributes of the created. Indeed, he is obliged to negate His essence too, since he can only conceive of essences as created essences.

It is known that the Lord, exalted and glorified is He, is not like any of them. This falsehood has been embraced by the extreme negators (ghulat al-mu'attilah). The more the negator goes to extremes in his negation, the more his statement becomes contradictory and its falsity evident, and it does not pass the test of sound reason, which does not err, except for what the messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, brought. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe, except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat: 159].

So He, exalted is He, declared Himself free of what everyone describes Him with, except His sincere servants, who are the messengers and those who follow them. As He said in another verse: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat: 180-182].

So He declared Himself free of what the describers describe Him with, and gave peace to the messengers for the soundness of what they described Him with, free of every deficiency and defect, and praised Himself, since He is the one described with the attributes of perfection for which praise is due, and free of every deficiency that contradicts the perfection of His praise.

(Section: On mentioning the well-known question among people and explaining what is in it)

It is that the Prophet ﷺ is superior to Ibrahim, so how did he request for himself the same prayer as Ibrahim's, when the thing likened to is originally supposed to be above the thing likened? How can these two contradictory matters be reconciled?

We will mention what people have said about this, and what in it is sound and what is unsound.

One group said: this prayer was taught by the Prophet ﷺ to his community before he knew that he was the master of the children of Adam. Whoever says this would have been better and more beneficial for himself had he remained silent. For this is the prayer that the Prophet ﷺ taught them when they asked him about the interpretation of ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

He taught them this prayer and made it legislated in the prayers of the community until the Day of Resurrection. The Prophet ﷺ was always the best of the children of Adam, before he knew of that and after he knew of it. And after he knew of it, he did not change the form of the prayer that he taught his community, nor replace it with another, nor was it narrated from him that anyone opposed it. So this is among the most corrupt of answers.

Another group said: this request and this supplication were legislated so that Allah would take him as a khalil (intimate friend), just as He took Ibrahim as a khalil, and Allah has answered him in that, as is established in the authentic reports: "Indeed, your companion is the khalil of the Most Merciful," meaning himself. This answer is of the same kind as the previous one, for its implication is that after Allah took him as a khalil, the prayer is no longer legislated upon him in this form. This is among the most false of falsehoods.

Another group said: this comparison refers to the one who prays, regarding the reward he obtains from the prayer upon him. So he asks his Lord for a reward, which is that He send blessings upon him as He sent blessings upon the family of Ibrahim, not in relation to the Prophet ﷺ. For what is sought for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of prayer is greater and more magnificent than what is attained by anyone else among the worlds.

This is of the same kind as the previous, and it is more corrupt, for the comparison does not concern what is attained by the one who prays, but what is attained by the one prayed for, who is the Prophet ﷺ. Whoever says that the meaning is "O Allah, give me from the reward of my prayer upon him as You sent blessings upon the family of Ibrahim" has distorted the words and erred in his speech.

Were it not that these aspects and their like have been mentioned by some commentators, who filled pages with them and made people think there is verification in them, it would have been better to turn away from them entirely and forgo mentioning them, for the scholar is ashamed to speak on this and occupy himself with refuting it.

Another group said: the comparison refers only to the family (al-al), and the sentence is complete at His saying "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad," then he said "and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Ibrahim." So the prayer requested for the family of Muhammad is the one compared to the prayer that the family of Ibrahim received. This was transmitted by al-Imrani from al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is certainly false as attributed to him, for al-Shafi'i is too great to say such a thing, and this does not befit his knowledge and eloquence, for it is in the extreme of weakness and feebleness.

Many hadiths of the chapter have already mentioned "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad as You sent blessings upon the family of Ibrahim," and the hadiths with this wording have already been cited.

Furthermore, it is not sound from the standpoint of Arabic grammar. When the governing word (al-'amil) is mentioned with its governed object (ma'mul), and another is coordinated with it, then it is qualified by an adverbial phrase, a prepositional phrase, a verbal noun, or an adjective of a verbal noun, that qualification refers to the governed object and not to what is coordinated with it. This is what Arabic does not permit otherwise. When you say "Zayd and 'Amr came to me on Friday," the adverb of time qualifies the coming of both of them, not the coming of 'Amr alone. Likewise if you say "I struck Zayd and 'Amr with a painful striking," or "in front of the amir," or "Zayd and 'Amr greeted me on Friday," and the like.

If you say: this holds when the governing word is not repeated; but when it is repeated, it is acceptable. You say "greet Zayd and greet 'Amr when you meet him," and it is not impossible that this is specific to 'Amr. Here the governing word has been repeated in His saying "and upon the family of Muhammad."

It is said: this example does not match the question of prayer. The matching example would be to say "greet Zayd and greet 'Amr as you greet the believers," and the like. In that case, the claim that the comparison is for his greeting of 'Amr alone and not Zayd is a false claim.

Another group said: it does not follow that the thing likened to must be higher than the thing likened; rather, it is permissible that the two be equal, and that the thing likened be higher than the thing likened to.

These said: the Prophet ﷺ is superior to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in respects other than prayer, even if they are equal in prayer. They said: the evidence that the thing likened may be superior to the thing likened to is the saying of the poet:

"Our sons are the sons of our sons, and our daughters' sons are the sons of distant men."

This view is also weak in several respects:

The first: this contradicts the established principle regarding likening one thing to another, for the Arabs liken a thing only to what is above it.

The second: the prayer from Allah, exalted is He, is among the highest of ranks and the most exalted, and Muhammad ﷺ is the best of creation. So the prayer that is attained by him must necessarily be better than every prayer attained by any created being, and no one else can be equal to him in it.

The third: Allah, glorified is He, after informing that He and His angels send blessings upon him, commanded the prayer and peace upon him, and emphasized it with the greeting (taslim). This information and command He has not established in the Qur'an for anyone else among the created.

The fourth: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the teacher of people good." This is because by teaching them good, they have rescued them from the evil of this world and the Hereafter, and have been the means of their success and happiness. And that is the cause of their entry into the body of believers upon whom Allah and His angels send blessings. Since the teachers of good are the means to the blessings of Allah and His angels upon those they teach, may Allah and His angels bless them. It is known that there is no one among the teachers of good who is greater, more abundant in teaching, more sincere to his community, or more patient in his teaching than the Prophet ﷺ. For this reason his community attained from his teaching what no other nation attained, and the community gained from their learning beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds, through which they became "the best nation brought forth for mankind." So how could the prayer upon this Messenger, the teacher of good, be equal to the prayer upon one who does not match him in this teaching?

As for their citation of the poet's verse as proof that the thing likened to may be superior to the thing likened, it does not prove that. For his saying "our sons are the sons of our sons" either has its subject placed later and its predicate placed earlier, and he likened the sons of his sons to his sons, and placing the predicate first is permitted here because the meaning is clear and no ambiguity occurs; and on this basis it runs according to the principle of comparison. Or it is of the type of reversed comparison, as one likens the moon to a person of perfect beauty, the lion to one perfect in courage, and the sea to one perfect in generosity, treating this man as the branch being likened. This is permissible when the reversal carries this meaning. On this basis this poet has placed the sons of his sons in the position of his sons, and that they are above them in his estimation, then likened his sons to them. This is the view of some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani). But what I hold concerning it is that the poet did not intend that. Rather he intended to distinguish between the sons of his sons and the sons of his daughters, so he informed that the sons of his daughters follow their fathers and are not "our sons." Our sons are only the sons of our sons, not the sons of our daughters. So he did not intend to liken the sons of his sons to his sons, nor the reverse; he intended only the meaning we have mentioned, and this is evident.

Another group said: the Prophet ﷺ has a prayer specific to him, which no prayer equals unless someone else shares in it, and what is requested for him is a prayer exceeding what has been given to him, joined to it; and that additional prayer is likened to the prayer upon Ibrahim. It is not objectionable that one asks for the superior a virtue given to the inferior, joined to what he himself has been specially given of virtue that others have not attained.

They said: an example of this is that a sultan gives one man a great deal of wealth and gives another less than that wealth, and then one asks the sultan to give the owner of the great wealth the like of what he gave the one below him, so that it is added to what he was given, and thus he obtains from the combination of the two gifts more than he would obtain from the great wealth alone.

This is also weak, because Allah, exalted is He, informed that He and His angels send blessings upon him, then commanded the prayer upon him. There is no doubt that what is requested from Allah is the like of the prayer that was reported, not something less than it, and the prayer that is most complete and most excellent upon him, not an inferior and lesser prayer. According to the view of these people, the request would only be for a lesser prayer, not a superior one, and it would become superior only by being joined to a prayer not requested. There is no doubt of the corruption of this, for the prayer that the community asks for him from his Lord is the most magnificent and most excellent prayer.

Another group said: the comparison mentioned refers only to the basic nature of the prayer, not to its measure or its manner. So what is requested refers to the form and not to the amount of what is bestowed. This is like when you say to a man, "Be good to your son as you were good to so-and-so," and you do not mean by that the measure of the goodness, but rather its basic nature. This may be supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

There is no doubt that no one can do good to the extent that Allah has done good to him; rather, what is meant is the basic nature of goodness, not its measure. Among them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa': 163].

This comparison concerns the basic nature of revelation, not its measure or the excellence of what is revealed.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then let him bring us a sign as the former messengers were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5].

What they meant is the kind of sign, not its equivalent.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth, just as He granted succession to those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them﴾ [al-Nur: 55].

It is known that the manner of succession differs, and that what this community has is more perfect than what others had.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 33, verse 56 (part 4 of 9):

The comparison is only in the basic principle of the act (ṣawm? no: of the act itself), not in its specific form, its measure, or its manner.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ [al-A'raf: 29].

It is well known that there is a difference between the first creation, which is the beginning, and the second, which is the return. Allah the Exalted also says: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15].

It is well known that the comparison lies in the basic fact of sending, and does not require that the two messengers be identical.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance He is due, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry and return in the evening full." So the comparison here is in the basic fact of provision, not in its measure or its manner, and there are many similar examples.

This answer is also weak, for several reasons.

Among them: what they have mentioned could be used for the higher, the lower, and the equal alike. If you say, "Be good to your father and your family just as you were good to your riding animal and your servant, and the like," that would be permissible. And it is well known that if the comparison were in the basic fact of prayer, it would be proper to say, "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, just as You sent prayers upon the family of Abu Awfa, or just as You sent prayers upon ordinary believers, and the like, or just as You sent prayers upon Adam, Noah, Hud and Lut." For according to these people the comparison is only in the basic fact of prayer, not in its measure or its quality.

There is no difference in this between anyone upon whom prayer is sent, and what distinction or virtue would there then be in this for Ibrahim and his family (ﷺ)? What would then be the benefit of mentioning him and mentioning his family? It would have sufficed to say, "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad," alone.

Second: the examples they cited are not analogous to the prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ). These examples are of two kinds: informative and imperative. As for those that are informative, the purpose of the comparison in them is argument, bringing the matter closer to understanding, and confirming that informative statement, which is something no intelligent person should deny, like the analogue of the thing compared to. So how can you deny the return when the beginning has been acknowledged, and it is its analogue, and the analogue carries the same ruling? For this reason, Allah the Exalted frequently argues from the beginning to the return.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ [al-A'raf: 29].

And He says: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104].

And He says: ﴿And he presents for Us an example and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?" Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time. And He is Knowing of all creation."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78-79].

This is abundant in the Qur'an.

Likewise the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15].

That is: how can you deny it, when messengers came before you from Me, bringing good news and warning, and you know what happened to those who disobeyed My messengers, how I seized them with a severe seizing?

Likewise the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa: 163].

That is: you are not the first messenger to come to the world. Rather, messengers came before you to whom I revealed just as I revealed to you. As Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "I am not a novelty among the messengers"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9].

This is a rebuttal and a denial directed at those who deny the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), though he came with the same kind of signs that the messengers before him brought, and even greater ones. How, then, can his messengership be denied? It is not one of the matters that are new to the world. Indeed, the earth has never been without messengers and their traces. Thus your messenger came in the path of those messengers who preceded him in messengership; he was not a novelty.

Likewise the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, just as He made successors those before them﴾ [al-Nur: 55].

This is information about His habit in creation and His wisdom, which does not change: that whoever believes and does righteous deeds will be firmly established by Him upon the earth and made successors in it, and He will not destroy them or cut off their posterity, just as He destroyed and cut off the posterity of those who denied His messengers and opposed them. Allah the Exalted thus informs them of His wisdom and His treatment of those who believe in His messengers and affirm them, and that He will deal with them as He dealt with those who came before them, the followers of the messengers. Similarly, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance He is due, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds," is information that Allah provides for those who rely upon Him from where they do not expect, and that He never leaves them without provision, just as you see with the birds: they go out from their nests hungry, and Allah provides for them until they return full from His provision. You are more honored before Allah than the birds and all other animals, so if you relied upon Him, He would provide for you from where you do not expect, and would not withhold His provision from any of you. This is of the category of information.

As for the category of command and request, the purpose in it is to draw attention to the cause, and that the reward is of the same kind as the deed. So when you say, "Teach as Allah taught you," or "Do good as Allah has done good to you" [al-Qasas: 77], or "Pardon as Allah pardoned you," and the like, it serves as a reminder to the one addressed to thank for the blessing that Allah has bestowed upon him, and that he is worthy to repay it with its like and to bind it with gratitude, for the recompense of that blessing is of its own kind. It is well known that addressing the Lord, glory be to Him, with any such thing is impermissible and not becoming to Him, so the mention of the comparison would be idle, having no benefit, and this is not permissible.

Third: His saying "as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim" is an attribute of a omitted verbal noun, and its meaning is "a prayer like Your prayer upon the family of Ibrahim." The literal sense of this speech is that the prayer should be similar to the prayer it is compared to, so one should not depart from the literal meaning of the speech and its intended sense.

Another group said that this comparison applies to every prayer of those who pray. So every worshipper who prays upon the Prophet (ﷺ) with this prayer has asked Allah to send prayers upon His Messenger (ﷺ) like the prayer given to the family of Ibrahim. There is no doubt that if he receives from every worshipper a request to Allah that He send him a prayer like His prayer upon the family of Ibrahim, he will receive from that multiples of prayers beyond count, and none comes close to him in this, let alone equals or surpasses him (ﷺ).

A parallel to this is a king who gives a man a thousand dirhams, and each of his subjects asks him to give another man something better than that, similar to those thousand. Each of them has asked him to give a thousand, so he receives thousands in number equal to the number of petitioners.

The proponents of this view raised an objection against themselves: the comparison applies to the basic fact of this requested prayer and to each of its individual instances, so the difficulty stands as it is.

Its statement: the gift given to the superior person must be better than the gift given to the inferior one, so if a gift is requested for him that is less than what he deserves, that is not fitting for his rank.

They answered this by saying that the difficulty arises only if the command is not for repetition. But if the command is for repetition, then what is required of the community is that they ask Allah to send prayers upon him, one prayer after another, each of which is similar to what was given to Ibrahim (peace be upon him). So he will receive prayers whose quantity cannot be counted, in comparison with the prayer given to Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

This is also weak, for the comparison here lies in the prayer of Allah upon him, not in the meaning of the worshipper's prayer. The meaning of this supplication, "O Allah, give him the like of what You gave Ibrahim," is that the one asked for should receive a prayer equal to the prayer upon Ibrahim. Whenever this request is repeated, this is its meaning. So every worshipper has asked Allah to send prayers upon him with a prayer less than what he deserves, and this request and the command to make it are repeated. Is this anything other than strengthening the side of the difficulty?

Moreover, the comparison applies to the basic fact of prayer and to its individual instances, and your answer about repetition does not remove it at all. Repetition does not make the side of the compared-to (the "mushabbah bihi") stronger than the side of the compared (the "mushabbah"), as the nature of comparison requires. Even if repetition made it so, the excuse by it would be beneficial. Rather, repetition requires increasing the superiority and strength of the compared (the "mushabbah"). So how can it then be compared to what is lower than it? Thus the weakness of this answer is made clear.

Another group said: the family of Ibrahim includes prophets, whom the family of Muhammad does not have the like of. So when a prayer is requested for the Prophet (ﷺ) and his family like that given to Ibrahim and his family, among whom are prophets, the family of the Prophet (ﷺ) receives what befits them, for they do not reach the ranks of the prophets. The excess that belongs to the prophets, among whom is Ibrahim, remains for Muhammad (ﷺ), and so he gains through it a distinction that no one else has gained.

The explanation of this is that the prayer given to Ibrahim and his family, among whom are prophets, is taken as a whole and divided between Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family. There is no doubt that the family of the Prophet (ﷺ) does not receive the like of what the family of Ibrahim received, among whom are prophets; rather, they receive what befits them. So the share of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the abundant excess that his family did not deserve remain exclusively his (ﷺ). Thus what he receives from the sum of all this is greater and more excellent than what Ibrahim received. This is better than everything that preceded it.

Better than this is to say: Muhammad (ﷺ) is himself from the family of Ibrahim, indeed he is the best of the family of Ibrahim, as ʿAli ibn Abi Talha narrated from Abu Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), concerning the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Ibrahim and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33].

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Muhammad is from the family of Ibrahim. This is an explicit statement. For if other prophets who are descendants of Ibrahim enter into his family, then the entry of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is more fitting. So our saying "as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim" includes sending prayers upon him and upon all the prophets who are descendants of Ibrahim.

Then Allah has commanded us to send prayers upon him and upon his family specifically, to the extent that we send prayers upon him together with all the family of Ibrahim in general, and he is among them. The family receives what befits them, and the remainder belongs entirely to him (ﷺ). The explanation of this is that he has been prayed for specifically and has been requested a prayer like that of the family of Ibrahim, while he is included with them. There is no doubt that the prayer given to the family of Ibrahim with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among them is more complete than the prayer given to him without them, so there is requested for him this great prayer, which is definitely better than what was given to Ibrahim. Then the purpose of the comparison and its operation on its basis becomes clear, and that the prayer requested for him by this wording is greater than that requested for him by other wording. For when what is requested by the supplication is only the like of the compared-to, and he has the fullest share of it, then he obtains from the compared-to what is greater than what Ibrahim and others obtained, and this is added to the share he has from the compared-to that others did not obtain.

Thus it becomes clear from this his excellence and nobility over Ibrahim and over every one of his family, among whom are the prophets, is what is fitting for him, and this prayer becomes indicative of this superiority, following it, and one of its requirements and implications. So (ﷺ) and upon his family, peace abundantly, and may He reward him on our behalf with the best reward given by any prophet on behalf of his community. O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious.

(Section: On mentioning a fine point regarding this hadith in which prayer upon him and his family is requested, as He sent prayer upon Ibrahim and his family.)

It is that most of the sound and good hadiths, indeed all of them, explicitly mention the Prophet (ﷺ) and mention his family. As for the one compared to, Ibrahim and his family, the reports came only with mention of the family of Ibrahim alone, without mentioning Ibrahim, or with mention of him alone without mentioning his family. No sound hadith has come containing the wording "Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim" as the wording "Muhammad and the family of Muhammad" is widely reported.

We shall cite the hadiths transmitted on this, then mention what Allah has facilitated regarding the secret of this.

We say: this hadith is in the Sahih in four ways.

The most famous of them is the hadith of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra met me and said, "Shall I not give you a gift? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us, and we said, 'We have known how to greet you; how shall we send prayers upon you?' He said, 'Say: O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious. O Allah, bless'" and in another wording, "And bless Muhammad as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious." Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal in the Musnad.

This is their wording, except al-Tirmidhi, who said: "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim," only, and likewise in the mention of blessing, without mentioning the family. This is a narration of Abu Dawud.

In another narration: "as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim," mentioning the family only, "as You blessed Ibrahim," mentioning him only.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Saʿidi: They said, "O Messenger of Allah, how shall we send prayers upon you?" He said, "Say: O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon his wives and his offspring, as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and his wives and his offspring, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious." This is the well-known wording.

It has also been narrated in it, "as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim, and as You blessed Ibrahim," without the word "family" in both places.

In al-Bukhari, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, this is the greeting upon you; how is the prayer upon you?" He said, "Say: O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad, Your servant and Your messenger, as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim."

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Masʿud al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to us while we were in the assembly of Saʿd ibn ʿUbada, and Bashir ibn Saʿd said to him, "Allah has commanded us to send prayers upon you; how shall we send prayers upon you?" He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell silent until we wished he had not asked him. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Say: O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, among the worlds, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious. And peace is as you have known."

This hadith has also been narrated with another wording, "as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim, and as You blessed Ibrahim," without mentioning the family in either.

In another narration, "as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim, and as You blessed the family of Ibrahim," mentioning Ibrahim alone in the first and the family alone in the second.

These are the well-known wordings in these hadiths. The most famous of them is the wording "the family of Ibrahim" in both places; in some of them the wording is "Ibrahim" in both places; in some, "Ibrahim" in the first and "the family" in the second; and in some, the reverse.

And as for combining Ibrahim with the family of Ibrahim: al-Bayhaqi narrated it in his Sunan from the hadith of Yahya ibn al-Sabbaq, from a man of the Banu al-Harith, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When one of you recites the tashahhud (the seated testimony recited in prayer) let him say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and have mercy upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings, blessed, and had mercy upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim; surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious." He said: "This chain is weak."

And al-Daraqutni narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Ishaq: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Abd Rabbih, from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him), and he mentioned the hadith, in which is: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious." Then he said: "This chain is good and continuous."

In al-Nasa'i, from the hadith of Musa ibn Talha, from his father, who said: "We said: O Messenger of Allah, how is the blessing upon you?" He said: "Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious." However, he related it in this form, and he related it in an abridged form, mentioning only Ibrahim in both places.

Ibn Majah also narrated another hadith, halted at Ibn Mas'ud (a report ending with a Companion rather than the Prophet), in which is Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. He said in the Sunan: al-Husayn ibn Bayan narrated to us, Ziyad ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, al-Mas'udi narrated to us, from Awn ibn Abd Allah, from Abu Fakhita, from al-Aswad ibn Yazid, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When you send blessings upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), do so well, for you do not know, perhaps that will be presented to him." He said: "They said to him: Then teach us." He said: "Say: O Allah, direct Your blessings, mercy and blessings upon the master of the Muslims, the leader of the God-fearing, the seal of the Prophets, Muhammad, Your servant and Messenger, the leader of goodness, the commander of goodness, and the Messenger of mercy. O Allah, raise him to a praiseworthy station which the first and the last will envy him for. O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious." And this is halted (a Companion's statement).

Most of the hadiths in the Sahih collections and the Sunan, as we mentioned at the start, limit themselves either to the family or to Ibrahim in both places, or to the family in one and Ibrahim in the other. This is also the case in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned earlier at the beginning of the book, and other hadiths. So wherever Ibrahim alone is mentioned in both places, this is because he is the origin of the blessing being reported, and his family are followers of him in it; so mention of the one followed indicates the follower, and he is included in it, and mention of him suffices without mentioning them. And wherever only his family is mentioned, this is because he is included within his family, as previously explained; so mention of the family of Ibrahim suffices without mentioning him, and mentioning both in two terms (is redundant). Wherever he is mentioned in one place alone and his family alone in the other, this is a combination of the two matters: he is mentioned, who is the origin, and his followers are mentioned with a term that includes him among them.

It remains to be said: why is Muhammad mentioned in conjunction in most hadiths, rather than limiting to one of them, while in most hadiths only Ibrahim and his family are mentioned?

The answer to that: the blessing upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and upon his family is mentioned in the context of request and supplication.

As for the blessing upon Ibrahim, it came in the context of report and the narration of an actual event.
